sections.body:
Clinical examination questions in the PPDS entrance examination test pattern recognition — the ability to map a set of physical findings to the correct diagnosis. The patterns are consistent, the traps are predictable, and the preparation is systematic.

## High-yield sign-diagnosis associations

Sign | Diagnosis | Mechanism
Fixed wide splitting of S2 | ASD | Equalised RA filling → fixed P2 delay
Collapsing pulse + early diastolic murmur (lean forward) | Aortic regurgitation | Wide pulse pressure + AR jet
Malar flush + loud S1 + opening snap + diastolic rumble at apex | Mitral stenosis | All from MS and its sequelae
Paradoxical splitting of S2 | LBBB, severe AS, RV pacing | Delayed A2 comes after P2
Pulsatile liver + giant v waves in JVP | Severe tricuspid regurgitation | Systolic regurgitant jet into RA/hepatic veins
Kussmaul's sign + elevated JVP + clear lungs + elevated JVP | RV infarction or constrictive pericarditis | Fixed pericardium or stiff RV cannot expand on inspiration
Mid-systolic click moving earlier with Valsalva/standing | Mitral valve prolapse | Smaller LV → earlier prolapse
Murmur louder with Valsalva, softer with squatting | HOCM | Dynamic LVOTO worsens with ↓ preload
Differential cyanosis (lower limbs only) | PDA-Eisenmenger | Right-to-left ductal flow into descending aorta
Continuous machinery murmur, infraclavicular | PDA | Continuous aorto-pulmonary pressure gradient
Single S2 + cyanosis + RV heave | TOF or severe PS | Absent/soft P2 from reduced pulmonary blood flow
Bisferiens pulse | Mixed AS+AR or HOCM | Two systolic peaks from anacrotic and tidal wave
Pulmonary ejection click louder in expiration | Pulmonary stenosis | Paradoxical — PV pre-opened by ↑ RV filling on inspiration
de Musset's sign + collapsing pulse + wide pulse pressure | Severe aortic regurgitation | Large stroke volume → head nodding
S3 + displaced apex + elevated JVP + crepitations | Biventricular heart failure | Left and right heart failure signs combined

## The 10 most frequently asked clinical examination question patterns

1. Which position enhances the AR murmur? → Lean forward, breath held in expiration, diaphragm at left sternal border
2. Which position enhances the MS rumble and S3? → Left lateral decubitus, bell of stethoscope at the apex
3. What happens to the HOCM murmur on Valsalva? → Increases (↓ preload → worsens LVOTO)
4. What happens to the MVP click on standing? → Moves earlier in systole (the murmur lengthens)
5. What is the Rivero-Carvalho sign? → TR murmur increases on inspiration (↑ RV filling → ↑ regurgitant volume)
6. Which S2 splitting pattern is pathognomonic of ASD? → Fixed wide splitting (does not change with respiration)
7. What is the significance of a palpable P2? → Always pathological — pulmonary hypertension
8. Can S4 be present in AF? → No — S4 requires organised atrial contraction
9. What is Kussmaul's sign and where is it seen? → JVP rises or fails to fall on inspiration; constrictive pericarditis, restrictive CMP, RV infarction, severe RHF
10. What is the significance of the Austin Flint murmur? → Mid-diastolic rumble in severe AR from functional MV obstruction by the AR jet — echoes like MS but no OS, no loud S1

## Quick reference — the OSCE cardiovascular examination sequence

Key concept: The complete 5-minute cardiovascular examination sequence for OSCE
1. General inspection: dyspnoea, cyanosis, pallor, cachexia, oedema visible
2. Hands: clubbing (Schamroth test), splinter haemorrhages, peripheral cyanosis, xanthomata, temperature
3. Radial pulse: rate, rhythm, character, volume; both radials simultaneously
4. Face: malar flush, corneal arcus, xanthelasma, conjunctival pallor/icterus
5. JVP: patient at 45°, measure height, waveform, AJR test
6. Carotid pulse: character (one side at a time), bruits
7. Blood pressure: both arms first visit; postural if indicated
8. Precordial inspection: scars, deformity, visible pulsations
9. Palpation: apex beat (location and character), parasternal heave, thrills (4 areas)
10. Auscultation — supine: 4 areas with diaphragm AND bell; S1, S2, murmurs, gallops
11. Auscultation — left lateral decubitus: apex with bell (S3, S4, MS rumble)
12. Auscultation — leaning forward: left sternal border with diaphragm (AR)
13. Dynamic auscultation: if HOCM or MVP suspected — Valsalva, squat/stand
14. Lung bases: auscultate posteriorly (crepitations, effusion)
15. Abdomen: hepatomegaly (size, tenderness, pulsatility), splenomegaly (IE), ascites
16. Legs: oedema (grade), peripheral pulses (all 8 pulses), venous changes
17. Thank and cover the patient; present findings with a summary and differential

sections.body:
The arterial pulse contains more information than a number. Rate, rhythm, volume, character, and symmetry — each component narrows the diagnostic field. The collapsing pulse of aortic regurgitation, the plateau pulse of aortic stenosis, and the pulsus paradoxus of tamponade are diagnoses carried in the examiner's fingers before a stethoscope is placed.

## The five components of every pulse assessment

1. Rate: count for 30 seconds × 2 (irregular rhythms require 60 seconds). Normal: 60–100 bpm. Bradycardia: <60 bpm. Tachycardia: >100 bpm.
2. Rhythm: regular, regularly irregular (e.g. bigeminy, Wenckebach), or irregularly irregular (AF — the gold standard bedside diagnosis of AF is the irregularly irregular pulse).
3. Volume: large volume (collapsing or bounding) or small volume (weak, thready). Note: volume and character are related but distinct.
4. Character: the waveform felt at the fingertip — its upstroke, peak, and descent. The character conveys the most haemodynamic information.
5. Symmetry: radio-radial delay (aortic coarctation, subclavian stenosis), radio-femoral delay (coarctation of aorta — femoral pulse arrives later than radial), interarm BP difference >20 mmHg (aortic dissection, subclavian stenosis).

## Pulse character — the diagnostic waveforms

Sign: Collapsing pulse (water-hammer pulse)
Character: rapid forceful upstroke, then rapid collapse — the pulse "collapses" under the fingertips. Felt as: a striking upward impulse with immediate fall — like a hammer hitting and immediately releasing. How to elicit: lift the patient's arm above the heart level with the palmar surface of your fingers wrapped around the forearm — the collapsing quality is dramatically amplified by gravity-unloading. Causes: aortic regurgitation (AR — the archetypal cause; wide pulse pressure from large stroke volume + rapid runoff into the LV), hyperthyroidism, severe anaemia, pregnancy, fever, patent ductus arteriosus, arteriovenous fistula. Associated signs of AR: wide pulse pressure (SBP - DBP >60 mmHg), Corrigan's sign (visible carotid pulsation), de Musset's sign (head nodding with each heartbeat), Duroziez's sign (to-and-fro murmur over the femoral artery when partially compressed).

Sign: Plateau pulse (slow-rising, anacrotic pulse)
Character: slow upstroke, prolonged peak, slow descent — the pulse rises slowly to a flat-topped plateau. Cause: severe aortic stenosis (AS) — the narrowed valve limits the rate of ejection → slow velocity of blood entering the aorta → slow rise, delayed peak, reduced amplitude. Also called: pulsus parvus et tardus (small and late). Anacrotic notch: a small shoulder or notch on the upstroke of the carotid pulse waveform, felt in very severe AS — the initial partial ejection creates the notch before the main peak. Best felt in the carotid artery (the brachial and radial pulses may feel nearly normal in elderly with stiff arteries — carotid is more reliable for AS assessment).

Sign: Bisferiens pulse
Character: two systolic peaks per cycle — felt as a "double-bang" with the fingertips in a single systolic phase. Causes: mixed AS+AR (most common — the two peaks represent the anacrotic peak and the tidal wave), hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM — initial rapid ejection peak before LVOTO worsens, then a second peak after). Clinical significance: a bisferiens pulse in HOCM is pathognomonic of the dynamic obstruction pattern.

Sign: Pulsus alternans
Character: alternating strong and weak beats in a regular rhythm. Mechanism: severe LV dysfunction → alternating high and low intracellular calcium → beat-to-beat variation in contractile force. Not a rhythm abnormality — rhythm is regular, but force alternates. Confirmed by: sphygmomanometry — inflate cuff above systolic pressure, slowly release — first hear only the stronger beats at a higher systolic BP, then as cuff deflates further you hear the weaker beats appearing at a lower systolic (difference typically >10 mmHg in clinically significant alternans). Significance: always indicates severe LV dysfunction and poor prognosis.

Sign: Pulsus paradoxus
Definition: an exaggerated fall in systolic BP (>10 mmHg) during normal inspiration. Mechanism: during inspiration → ↑ RV filling → RV expands → interventricular septum shifts leftward (ventricular interdependence) → ↓ LV filling → ↓ CO → ↓ SBP. This is exaggerated in: cardiac tamponade (fixed pericardial volume → any RV expansion comes directly at LV expense), massive PE, tension pneumothorax, severe COPD/asthma. Measurement technique: inflate cuff above systolic → deflate slowly → note the pressure at which Korotkoff sounds are heard only on expiration → note the pressure at which sounds are heard throughout the cycle → the difference is pulsus paradoxus. >10 mmHg = significant (tamponade threshold: typically >12–15 mmHg with haemodynamic effects).

## Radio-radial and radio-femoral delay

Radio-radial delay: Simultaneous palpation of both radial pulses. A difference in timing or volume between right and left radial pulses indicates: subclavian artery stenosis or occlusion (Takayasu's arteritis, thoracic outlet syndrome), aortic arch aneurysm or dissection (Type A dissection can compress the left subclavian). A significant interarm BP difference (>20 mmHg systolic) accompanies the delay.

Radio-femoral delay: Simultaneous palpation of the right radial and right femoral pulse. Normally they are nearly simultaneous (the femoral pulse is physiologically slightly later in some individuals, but the difference is imperceptible). A clearly delayed femoral pulse, with the radial arriving noticeably before the femoral, indicates coarctation of the aorta. Also: lower limb BP is significantly less than upper limb BP (normal: leg BP 10–20 mmHg higher than arm).

Warning: Most common pulse examination mistakes:
1. Counting the pulse for only 15 seconds × 4 in an irregular rhythm — this introduces up to 25% error. Always count for 60 seconds in irregular rhythms.
2. Not comparing both radial pulses simultaneously — missing radio-radial delay.
3. Forgetting to lift the arm to elicit a collapsing pulse — the character may be near-normal at heart level in mild-moderate AR.
4. Confusing the carotid for the JVP — leading to an incorrect report of an elevated "carotid pulse" when the patient actually has a raised JVP with prominent v waves.

sections.body:
The JVP is a window directly into the right atrium. It provides real-time information about right heart filling pressure, rhythm, and the competence of the tricuspid valve — all without a single blood test or imaging study. It is the most examined and most commonly misinterpreted sign in cardiology.

## Measurement technique — the correct method

Key concept: Position: patient at 45°. Use the internal jugular vein — never the external jugular.
The internal jugular vein (IJV) runs deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle — you see its transmitted pulsation rather than the vein itself, as an undulating movement behind/between the two heads of the SCM. The external jugular vein (EJV) is more superficial and visible, but is less reliable because its valves and angulation can give falsely elevated readings. Always use the IJV. Position: patient reclining at 45° to the horizontal. The reference point for JVP measurement is the sternal angle of Louis (manubriosternal junction) — add 5 cm to get the right atrial level (since the RA is approximately 5 cm below the sternal angle in this position). Lighting: tangential lighting (from the side) reveals the pulsation best — overhead lighting washes it out. Ask the patient to relax their neck muscles. Turn their head slightly to the left.

## Measuring JVP height

Identify the upper border of the JVP pulsation (the top of the column of blood). Measure the vertical distance from the sternal angle to this upper border. Normal JVP height: 0–3 cm above the sternal angle (= 5–8 cm above the RA). JVP >3 cm above the sternal angle = elevated = raised RA pressure.

If the JVP is not visible at 45°: try 30° or even 15° (very elevated JVP may only be visible when nearly horizontal) or sit the patient upright at 90° (very low JVP may only be visible when nearly supine). The fact that the JVP disappears when the patient sits fully upright at 90° confirms it is truly venous (the column of blood falls below the clavicle).

## The JVP waveform — a, c, v waves and x, y descents

Component | Timing | Mechanism | Abnormality
a wave | Just before S1 (presystolic) | Atrial contraction → RA pressure rises | Large a wave: tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary hypertension, RV hypertrophy (atrium contracting against resistance); Absent a wave: atrial fibrillation (no organised atrial contraction); Cannon a wave: atrium contracts against closed TV (complete heart block, VT, junctional rhythm)
c wave | Shortly after S1 | Tricuspid valve bulges back into RA as RV contracts | Usually not visible clinically; merges with the a-x descent
x descent | Mid-systole | RA relaxation + TV leaflets pulled down as RV contracts and shortens | Absent x descent: cardiac tamponade (dominant y descent gives characteristic pattern); prominent x descent: tamponade (early stage)
v wave | End of systole (just before S2) | Venous return fills the RA while TV is closed | Large/giant v wave: tricuspid regurgitation (regurgitant jet → RA fills from below and above → massive systolic RA pressure rise visible as giant v wave); also seen in non-compliant RA, atrial septal defect
y descent | Early diastole (after S2) | TV opens → RA empties into RV | Slow y descent: tricuspid stenosis; Sharp y descent: constrictive pericarditis, restrictive CMP, severe RHF; Absent y descent: tamponade

## Kussmaul's sign

Sign: Kussmaul's sign
Definition: paradoxical rise (or failure to fall) of the JVP on inspiration. Normal physiology: inspiration → ↓ intrathoracic pressure → ↑ venous return to the right heart → RA accommodates the extra volume by expanding → JVP falls. Kussmaul's sign: the right heart cannot accommodate the increased venous return → JVP rises or fails to fall. Causes: constrictive pericarditis (rigid pericardium prevents RV expansion), restrictive cardiomyopathy, right ventricular failure (severe), right ventricular infarction (stiff, infarcted RV wall). NOT seen in: cardiac tamponade (the JVP in tamponade fluctuates normally or rises on expiration — the opposite). Kussmaul's sign + elevated JVP + clear lungs = classic RV infarction or constrictive pericarditis triad.

## Abdominojugular reflux (AJR) — technique and interpretation

Technique: apply firm, sustained pressure over the right upper quadrant (or mid-abdomen) for 15 seconds while observing the JVP. Instruct the patient to breathe normally (not hold their breath — Valsalva from breath-holding falsely elevates the JVP). A rise of >3 cm in JVP that is sustained throughout the 15-second pressure period = positive AJR.

Interpretation: positive AJR indicates elevated right atrial pressure (right heart failure, cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, restrictive CMP) or right ventricular dysfunction. It is a sensitive indicator of elevated LVEDP when combined with other signs of left heart failure — the excess venous return unmasks a borderline right heart that cannot cope with the extra preload.

Warning: Most common JVP examination mistakes:
1. Using the external jugular vein instead of the internal jugular — EJV has valves and can be falsely elevated. Always specify which vein you are assessing.
2. Measuring the horizontal distance instead of the vertical distance from the sternal angle — only the vertical height reflects hydrostatic pressure.
3. Confusing the JVP with the carotid pulse — press lightly at the base of the neck (abolishes venous pulsation, not carotid).
4. Not performing the abdominojugular reflux test — often omitted, often tested in the examination.
5. Saying "hepatojugular reflux" — the correct term is abdominojugular reflux (AJR). The liver itself is not needed; abdominal compression anywhere works.

sections.body:
Blood pressure measurement is the most performed clinical procedure in medicine — and one of the most frequently performed incorrectly. The errors in technique are systematic and predictable. Equally important are the special BP measurements that carry diagnostic weight: postural BP, pulsus paradoxus, and the ankle-brachial index.

## Standard BP measurement — the errors that change management

Error | Effect on reading | Correction
Cuff too small for arm circumference | Falsely HIGH by 5–15 mmHg | Cuff bladder should encircle ≥80% of arm circumference. Use large adult cuff in obese patients.
Cuff too large | Falsely LOW | Use appropriately sized cuff
Arm below heart level | Falsely HIGH (~2 mmHg per 2.5 cm below) | Support the arm at mid-sternal level
Arm above heart level | Falsely LOW | Support at mid-sternal level
Patient not rested (5 min sitting) | Falsely HIGH (sympathetic activation) | Patient seated, rested ≥5 min, no caffeine or smoking for ≥30 min
Talking during measurement | Falsely HIGH by 10–15 mmHg | No conversation during measurement
Crossed legs | Falsely HIGH by 5–8 mmHg (increases venous return and CO) | Feet flat on floor, uncrossed
Deflating cuff too quickly | Underestimates systolic, overestimates diastolic | Deflate at 2 mmHg/second or 2 mmHg/heartbeat
Failing to check both arms on first visit | Missing interarm difference >20 mmHg (dissection, subclavian stenosis) | Always measure both arms on first visit; use the higher arm for subsequent readings

## Postural (orthostatic) blood pressure — technique

Key concept: Postural hypotension: SBP falls ≥20 mmHg or DBP falls ≥10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing
Technique: measure BP supine after ≥5 minutes lying down → ask the patient to stand → measure at 1 minute and 3 minutes standing. Report: the values and the symptoms (dizziness, presyncope, syncope). A fall within the first minute indicates neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (rapid autonomic failure — Parkinson's, diabetes). A fall at 3 minutes indicates delayed orthostatic hypotension (slower impairment of compensatory mechanisms). Clinical significance: increases fall risk 2× in elderly; associated with ischaemic stroke (nocturnal hypoperfusion); seen with: volume depletion, antihypertensive overdose, autonomic neuropathy (DM, Parkinson's, amyloidosis), prolonged bed rest, adrenal insufficiency, alpha-blocker therapy.

## Pulsus paradoxus — formal measurement

Inflation: pump cuff 20 mmHg above systolic (no sounds heard). Deflation: release at 2 mmHg/s. Listen carefully with the stethoscope over the brachial artery:

1. Note the pressure at which Korotkoff sounds are first heard — but only intermittently (during expiration)
2. Continue deflating. Note the pressure at which sounds are heard continuously throughout the respiratory cycle (both inspiration AND expiration)
3. The difference between these two pressures = pulsus paradoxus

Normal: <10 mmHg difference. Significant: >10 mmHg (tamponade, massive PE, severe COPD/asthma, tension PTX). Tamponade threshold: typically >12–15 mmHg with haemodynamic compromise.

## Ankle-brachial index (ABI) — the bedside PAD screen

ABI = highest ankle SBP (posterior tibial or dorsalis pedis) ÷ highest brachial SBP. Use a hand-held Doppler probe. Measure SBP in both arms and both ankles (4 measurements). ABI interpretation:

ABI value | Interpretation | Clinical implication
>1.40 | Non-compressible arteries (calcified) | Falsely elevated — seen in DM, CKD, elderly. Use toe pressure or pulse volume recording instead.
1.00–1.40 | Normal | PAD unlikely
0.91–0.99 | Borderline | Repeat with exercise ABI or Doppler waveform analysis
0.71–0.90 | Mild PAD | Claudication likely; ASCVD risk elevated
0.41–0.70 | Moderate PAD | Claudication or rest pain; urgent vascular assessment
≤0.40 | Severe PAD / critical limb ischaemia | Rest pain or tissue loss; urgent revascularisation

title: Blood pressure measurement and special techniques

sections.body:
Before the stethoscope touches the chest, the hands and eyes have already yielded valuable findings. The character and position of the apex beat, the presence of heaves and thrills, and the surface anatomy of the precordium each carry diagnostic weight that enhances auscultation rather than replacing it.

## Precordial inspection

- Surgical scars: midline sternotomy scar (CABG, valve replacement, congenital repair), lateral thoracotomy scar (older mitral surgery technique, coarctation repair, BT shunt), infraclavicular scar (pacemaker/ICD implantation), subcostal port scars (minimally invasive cardiac surgery).
- Chest deformity: pectus excavatum (concave sternum — may displace the apex, associated with MVP, Marfan syndrome); pectus carinatum (convex, "pigeon chest"); kyphoscoliosis (can displace the apex and cause pulmonary hypertension).
- Visible pulsations: visible apex beat in thin patients (normal); visible parasternal pulsation (RV enlargement); visible epigastric pulsation (abdominal aortic aneurysm or normal in thin individuals — distinguish by pulsation direction: AAA pulsates outward in all directions; normal aorta mainly anteriorly).

## The apex beat — character and position

Key concept: The apex beat: lowest and outermost point of definite cardiac impulse. Normally in the 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line.
Technique: feel with the flat of the fingertips, with the patient first supine, then turning to the left lateral decubitus position (which brings a normally positioned heart closer to the chest wall and amplifies the impulse). Identify: the position (ICS and distance from midline or MCL), the character (see below), and whether it is localised or diffuse.
A displaced apex (below the 5th ICS or lateral to the MCL) indicates cardiac enlargement (LV dilation in AR, DCM, longstanding MR) or a shift from an extracardiac cause (pleural effusion, pneumothorax). The cardiac diagnosis is suggested by the apex character.

Apex character | Description | Clinical significance
Normal | Localised, tapping, occupies one intercostal space, lasts <2/3 of systole | Normal LV
Heaving / sustained / pressure-loaded | Forceful, sustained throughout systole, well-localised — pushes against the fingers and maintains the pressure | LV pressure overload: severe AS, hypertensive LVH, HOCM. The LV is fighting a high afterload — it contracts powerfully and slowly.
Hyperdynamic / volume-loaded | Forceful, rapid, brief — strikes forcefully then immediately withdraws. Displaced laterally. Also called "thrusting" apex. | LV volume overload: AR, MR, VSD, high-output states (anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy). Large stroke volume → forceful but quick ejection.
Tapping apex | A sharp, brief, palpable impulse — feels like a "tap" rather than a push | Mitral stenosis — the palpable S1 (the loud S1 of MS) transmitted to the chest wall. Not a true apex beat character but a clinical sign.
Double impulse | Two distinct impulses felt per systole at the apex | HOCM (initial ejection peak then a second impulse from the obstructed residual ejection); palpable S4 gallop (presystolic impulse from atrial kick into a stiff LV)
Absent / impalpable | Cannot be located | Obesity, COPD (hyperinflated chest), pericardial effusion, dextrocardia (check right side!)

## Parasternal heave (right ventricular heave)

Sign: Parasternal heave
Technique: place the heel of the right hand (hypothenar eminence) firmly over the left parasternal region (2–4th intercostal spaces, 1–2 cm left of the sternum). A heave is a sustained, lifting outward movement that lifts the heel of the hand with each systole. Cause: right ventricular hypertrophy or dilation → the enlarged RV pushing anteriorly against the chest wall with each systolic contraction. Conditions: pulmonary hypertension (all causes), severe pulmonary stenosis, ASD with large shunt, tetralogy of Fallot, large anterior MI (LV to RV shift of the septum), severe TR. Distinguish from epigastric pulsation: the parasternal heave is clearly in the left parasternal region; epigastric pulsation is felt below the xiphisternum and may be from the aorta or the RV apex.

## Thrills — palpable murmurs

Sign: Thrill
A palpable murmur — felt as a vibration (like purring of a cat or the sensation of water rushing over fingers in a stream) over the precordium. A thrill indicates at least a grade 4/6 murmur. Location and timing identify the cause: (1) Systolic thrill at the right upper sternal border (RUSB) → aortic stenosis; (2) Systolic thrill at the left upper sternal border (LUSB) → pulmonary stenosis; (3) Systolic thrill at the lower left sternal border (LLSB) or pansystolic → VSD; (4) Diastolic thrill at the apex (rare) → severe MS; (5) Systolic thrill at the apex → severe MR. Always report a thrill — it fundamentally changes the grade of murmur and the clinical significance.

Warning: Palpation mistakes:
1. Reporting the apex beat position without specifying both ICS and distance from a reference line (MCL or midline) — this is incomplete.
2. Not attempting to feel the apex in the left lateral decubitus position — you will miss a subtle or impalpable apex that becomes clear with position change.
3. Missing a parasternal heave by using only fingertips — use the heel of the hand for heave assessment.
4. Not systematically feeling for thrills at each auscultatory area (aortic, pulmonary, tricuspid, mitral) before auscultating — a thrill in the wrong area reorients the auscultatory diagnosis.
5. Confusing a transmitted murmur thrill with a true parasternal heave — a thrill is a vibration, a heave is a lifting motion.

sections.body:
S1 and S2 are the boundaries of systole — the opening and closing brackets. Understanding their loudness, splitting, and relationship to each other is the foundation of all cardiac auscultation. Every subsequent murmur is timed against them.

## Auscultation technique — first principles

- Stethoscope selection: the diaphragm (flat surface) picks up high-pitched sounds (S1, S2, aortic/pulmonic murmurs, MR murmur, AS murmur). The bell (cup-shaped) picks up low-pitched sounds (S3, S4, MS diastolic rumble) — apply with very light pressure to the skin (firm pressure converts it to a diaphragm). If using an electronic stethoscope: low-frequency mode = bell equivalent.
- Auscultatory areas: Aortic (2nd right ICS, RSB), Pulmonic (2nd left ICS, LSB), Tricuspid (4th/5th left ICS, LSB), Mitral (apex, 5th ICS, MCL). These are transmission areas — not the anatomical valve locations. Also auscultate in the axilla (MR) and carotids (AS radiation).
- Positions: sit up and lean forward (enhances AR diastolic murmur — brings the aortic root closer to the chest wall); left lateral decubitus (brings apex closer → enhances S3, S4, MS rumble); supine (routine auscultation).
- Timing: palpate the carotid pulse simultaneously — it coincides with S1 and systole. Any sound coinciding with the carotid pulse = systolic. Any sound between the carotid pulses = diastolic.

## First heart sound (S1)

S1 is caused by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the beginning of systole. Mitral closure (M1) occurs slightly before tricuspid closure (T1) — normally heard as a single sound. Heard loudest at the apex.

S1 characteristic | Mechanism | Conditions
Loud S1 | Mitral leaflets are widely open at the moment of ventricular contraction → they must travel a long distance to close → high-velocity closure → loud S1 | Mitral stenosis (leaflets held open by gradient, snap shut → loud S1 + opening snap); tachycardia (short diastole → MV not fully closed at end of diastole); hyperdynamic states (fever, anaemia, exercise)
Soft S1 | Mitral leaflets are already nearly closed when systole begins → low-velocity, low-energy closure | First-degree AV block (long PR → MV floats toward closure before the forceful ventricular contraction); MR (MV doesn't close properly → soft closure); severe LV dysfunction (poor contractile force)
Variable S1 | Varying relationship between atrial and ventricular contraction → varying MV position at onset of systole | Complete heart block (P waves independent of QRS → sometimes favourable, sometimes unfavourable MV position); AF (varying RR intervals → varying diastolic filling → varying MV position)
Wide splitting of S1 | Delayed T1 (tricuspid closure) | RBBB, tricuspid stenosis, Ebstein's anomaly

## Second heart sound (S2) and splitting

S2 is caused by closure of the aortic valve (A2) followed by the pulmonic valve (P2). Normally A2 precedes P2 because: LV depolarises first (or simultaneously with RV), and aortic pressure is higher than pulmonary pressure so the aortic valve snaps shut first. On inspiration: ↑ venous return to RV → ↑ RV stroke volume → RV takes longer to empty → delayed P2 → physiological splitting of S2. On expiration: the two components come together → single S2.

S2 splitting pattern | Mechanism | Conditions | Exam trap
Physiological splitting | A2–P2 split widens on inspiration, narrows/disappears on expiration | Normal in young individuals | Must disappear on expiration — if it persists, it is abnormal
Wide fixed splitting | A2 and P2 are split on both inspiration and expiration, with fixed or near-fixed gap | ASD — the extra atrial shunt equalises RA filling regardless of respiratory phase → RV filling and ejection time remain constant → fixed P2 delay | Fixed splitting is PATHOGNOMONIC of ASD. The split does not change with respiration.
Wide (non-fixed) splitting | A2–P2 split present in expiration + widens on inspiration | RBBB (delayed RV conduction → delayed P2); pulmonary stenosis (delayed RV emptying → delayed P2) | Unlike fixed splitting of ASD, the gap changes with respiration
Paradoxical (reversed) splitting | P2 precedes A2 (reverse of normal). Split audible on expiration, disappears on inspiration | LBBB (delayed LV conduction → delayed A2, which now comes after P2); severe AS (delayed LV ejection → delayed A2); RV pacing; HOCM | The diagnostic clue: split heard on expiration, single sound on inspiration — the opposite of normal physiology
Loud P2 | High pulmonary artery pressure → pulmonic valve snaps shut with greater force | Pulmonary hypertension (any cause: IPAH, Eisenmenger, severe MS, COPD). Loud P2 palpable at the left upper sternal border is a reliable sign of significant pulmonary hypertension. | A palpable P2 is always pathological
Single S2 | One component is absent or inaudible | Severe AS (inaudible A2 from calcified immobile valve), pulmonary atresia (absent P2), Fallot (absent P2), elderly (normal) | Always note which component is absent if you can determine it

Clinical link: How to reliably time S1 and S2: If you cannot tell which sound is S1 and which is S2, palpate the carotid artery simultaneously. The carotid upstroke coincides with ventricular systole and follows S1 closely. S1 is the sound at the onset of the carotid pulse. S2 is the sound at the end of systole, just before the diastolic pause. In tachycardia where systole and diastole are nearly equal: listen at the base (aortic area) — S2 is always louder there than S1. At the apex: S1 is louder than S2. This physiological rule helps when timing is difficult.
sections.title: Study text

sections.body:
Added sounds are the cardiovascular equivalent of whispered additional information. S3 tells you the ventricle is volume-overloaded or failing. S4 tells you it is stiff. The opening snap announces a calcified but still-mobile mitral valve. The mid-systolic click announces a prolapsing leaflet. Each sound carries its own diagnostic narrative.

## Third heart sound (S3) — the ventricular gallop

Sign: Third heart sound (S3)
Timing: early diastole, shortly after S2. Forms the cadence: S1 – S2 – S3, like "Ken-TUCK-y" (stress on the first syllable = S3). Pitch: low-pitched — must use the bell of the stethoscope with very light pressure. Best heard: at the apex, with the patient in left lateral decubitus, listening with the bell. Mechanism: abrupt deceleration of ventricular filling in early diastole when the ventricle suddenly becomes non-distensible → vibration of the ventricular walls → low-frequency sound. Pathological S3: in adults, S3 indicates: LV systolic dysfunction (HFrEF — the most common cause in cardiology; the ventricle dilates, wall tension increases, abrupt deceleration occurs earlier), volume overload (MR, AR, VSD), or constrictive pericarditis (a specific, early, high-pitched S3 called a pericardial knock). Physiological S3: normal in children and young adults (<40 years) — simply indicates rapid ventricular filling in a compliant, vigorously contracting ventricle. An S3 in a 20-year-old athlete is normal; in a 55-year-old with hypertension and exertional dyspnoea, it is pathological and requires urgent investigation.

## Fourth heart sound (S4) — the atrial gallop

Sign: Fourth heart sound (S4)
Timing: late diastole, just before S1 (presystolic). Forms the cadence: S4 – S1 – S2, like "TEN-nes-see" (stress on the last syllable = S4). Pitch: low-pitched — use the bell. Mechanism: atrial contraction ("kick") against a non-compliant (stiff) ventricle → vibration of the ventricular walls as blood is forcibly expelled into the stiff LV. S4 requires: (1) a functioning atrium (never present in AF — there is no organised atrial contraction); (2) a stiff, non-compliant ventricle. Causes: LV hypertrophy (hypertension, AS, HOCM), acute MI (acutely stiff ischaemic myocardium → S4 occurs in almost all acute MIs with preserved sinus rhythm), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, acute severe AR or MR (acutely overloaded ventricle). Key rule: S4 in AF = impossible. If you hear a 4-sound complex in AF, the 4th sound is a summation gallop (S3 and S4 merge when the heart rate is fast enough that diastole is shortened).

## Ejection sounds (ejection clicks)

Sound | Timing | Best heard | Cause | Respiratory variation
Aortic ejection click | Early systole (immediately after S1) | Apex AND aortic area (transmits widely) | Bicuspid aortic valve (most common), dilated aorta, AS (if valve still mobile) | No change with respiration
Pulmonary ejection click | Early systole (immediately after S1) | Upper left sternal border (pulmonic area), varies with respiration | Pulmonary stenosis (the click of PS is the most common cause), pulmonary arterial hypertension, dilated pulmonary artery | DECREASES (or disappears) on inspiration — diagnostic! In inspiration, ↑ venous return → the PV partially opens during atrial systole → less distance to open fully in early RV systole → softer click

## The opening snap (OS) — mitral stenosis

Sign: Opening snap
Timing: early diastole, shortly after S2. The sequence: S1 – S2 – [OS] – diastolic rumble. Mechanism: in mitral stenosis, the thickened but still-mobile mitral valve leaflets are held shut by the high LA-LV pressure gradient throughout systole → at the moment of MV opening in early diastole, the leaflets snap open suddenly → brief, sharp, high-pitched early diastolic sound. Pitch: high-pitched — use the diaphragm. Location: loudest at the lower left sternal border and medial to the apex; radiates widely. Timing clue — S2-OS interval: the shorter the S2-OS interval, the higher the LA pressure (more severe MS). In severe MS: S2-OS <70 ms (barely audible gap). In mild MS: S2-OS >120 ms (clearly audible gap). Absent OS: if the MV leaflets are heavily calcified and immobile — there is no snap (the loud S1 also disappears). Absent OS in MS therefore suggests advanced calcification. Distinguish from S3: OS is higher-pitched (use diaphragm); heard in early diastole; followed by the diastolic rumble of MS. S3 is lower-pitched (use bell); heard slightly later in diastole; not followed by a rumble.

## Mid-systolic click — mitral valve prolapse

Sign: Mid-systolic click
Timing: mid-systole. Followed by a late systolic murmur (the MR resulting from the prolapsing valve). Mechanism: redundant, myxomatous mitral valve leaflets → one or both prolapse posteriorly into the LA in mid-systole → the chordae tighten suddenly → audible click. Dynamic variation — the key diagnostic tool for MVP:
• Standing / Valsalva (↓ preload → smaller LV → leaflets prolapse earlier) → click moves earlier in systole (toward S1); murmur lengthens.
• Squatting / Leg raise (↑ preload → larger LV → leaflets prolapse later) → click moves later in systole (toward S2); murmur shortens.
This movement of the click with dynamic maneuvers is PATHOGNOMONIC of MVP. No other click moves this way.

title: Added heart sounds: S3, S4, clicks, and snaps

sections.body:
Systolic murmurs are the most common auscultatory finding in cardiology practice. Their characterisation — timing, quality, radiation, grading, and dynamic response — determines whether you are dealing with a haemodynamically significant lesion requiring intervention or a benign flow murmur requiring only reassurance.

## Murmur characterisation — the six dimensions

1. Timing: systolic (between S1 and S2), diastolic, or continuous
2. Location: where loudest (apex, LUSB, RUSB, LLSB)
3. Radiation: where does it transmit? (carotids for AS, axilla for MR)
4. Quality/character: harsh, blowing, rumbling, musical, high-pitched
5. Grade: 1–6 (see below)
6. Dynamic response: changes with Valsalva, squatting, inspiration, isometric handgrip

## Murmur grading (Levine scale)

Grade | Description | Thrill?
1/6 | Barely audible, even with stethoscope in ideal conditions | No
2/6 | Soft but clearly audible | No
3/6 | Moderately loud, easily audible | No
4/6 | Loud | Yes — always
5/6 | Very loud — audible with stethoscope barely on chest | Yes
6/6 | Audible without stethoscope | Yes

## Ejection systolic murmur (ESM) — crescendo-decrescendo

Starts after S1 (gap between S1 and murmur onset), rises to a peak in mid-systole, then falls back, ending before S2. The "diamond shape" on phonocardiogram. Caused by turbulent flow through a semi-obstructive orifice during LV or RV ejection.

Cause | Location | Radiation | Distinguishing features
Aortic stenosis (AS) | RUSB (2nd right ICS) | Carotids (bilateral); also to apex | Slow-rising pulse; soft/absent A2; loud → severe AS; S4 common; Gallavardin phenomenon: the harsh component at RUSB, musical component at apex (may mimic MR)
Pulmonary stenosis (PS) | LUSB (2nd left ICS) | Left shoulder/back | Pulmonary ejection click precedes murmur; click diminishes on inspiration; P2 soft/delayed; RV heave; right heart signs
HOCM | LLSB and apex | Does NOT radiate to carotids (key distinction from AS) | Increases with Valsalva and standing (↓ preload); decreases with squatting (↑ preload); bisferiens carotid pulse
ASD | LUSB (pulmonary flow murmur) | Limited | Fixed wide splitting of S2; not a murmur from the ASD itself but from ↑ pulmonary flow across the PV
Innocent / flow murmur | LUSB or apex | None or minimal | Grade ≤2/6; no thrill; no radiation; normal S2; diminishes or disappears with standing (↓ preload); young, thin, no cardiac symptoms

## Pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur

Occupies the entire systole — begins with S1, occupies all of systole, and continues up to (and may obscure) S2. The pressure difference driving the regurgitation/shunt is present throughout systole.

Cause | Location | Radiation | Quality and features
Mitral regurgitation (MR) | Apex | Left axilla (classic); also to the back in posterior leaflet MR; radiates to the LUSB in anterior leaflet or chordal rupture | Blowing, high-pitched. Hyperdynamic displaced apex. S3 common. Reduced S1. Does NOT vary with respiration.
Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) | LLSB (4th/5th left ICS, lower sternum) | Right lateral chest; sometimes epigastrium | Blowing, high-pitched. Increases on inspiration (Rivero-Carvalho sign — more RV filling on inspiration → more regurgitation → louder murmur). Giant v waves in JVP. Pulsatile liver. RV heave.
VSD | LLSB (left sternal border) | Thrill usually present; may radiate all over precordium | Harsh, loud. Grade 4–5/6 typical. A thrill is almost always palpable. Small VSD = louder murmur ("maladie de Roger" — Roger's disease).

## Late systolic murmur

Starts after mid-systole and extends to S2. The classic cause is mitral valve prolapse (MVP): the click of the prolapsing leaflet is followed by the late systolic MR murmur as the leaflets prolapse into the LA and fail to coapt. With dynamic maneuvers: click and murmur onset move earlier with Valsalva/standing (smaller LV → earlier prolapse).

Clinical link: Gallavardin phenomenon (AS): In severe aortic stenosis, the murmur may have two components that are heard as if they originate from different places — a harsh, noisy component at the right upper sternal border (the typical AS location) AND a musical, high-pitched component at the apex. The apical component can be mistaken for MR. Distinguish: (1) the apical component of Gallavardin has a musical quality rather than blowing; (2) it does NOT radiate to the axilla (MR does); (3) the slow-rising pulse and other AS signs are present; (4) dynamic maneuvers: squat → both components of AS increase (preload ↑ → more flow through stenotic valve); Valsalva → both decrease. MR murmur increases with squatting only minimally. Always report the Gallavardin phenomenon when present.

sections.body:
Diastolic murmurs are never innocent in adults — every diastolic murmur requires a diagnosis. The high-pitched decrescendo murmur of aortic regurgitation, the low-pitched rumble of mitral stenosis, and the continuous machine-like sound of PDA each have a distinctive character that, once learned, is instantly recognisable.

## Early diastolic murmurs — high-pitched and decrescendo

Sign: Aortic regurgitation (AR) — early diastolic murmur
Timing: immediately after S2 (begins with aortic valve closure), decrescendo throughout diastole. Pitch: high-pitched, blowing — use the diaphragm firmly. Best heard: leaning forward, breath held in expiration (brings the aortic root closer to the chest wall), diaphragm at the left sternal border (3rd/4th ICS) — this is the only murmur that requires the patient to lean forward. Also heard at the right sternal border (if the aortic root is dilated — aortic root disease). Duration and severity: in severe AR, the murmur is longer (decrescendo throughout diastole) and louder (higher regurgitant flow). In very severe, acute AR: the murmur may actually become shorter (LV pressure rapidly equilibrates with aortic pressure → the gradient driving regurgitation vanishes early in diastole).

Sign: Pulmonary regurgitation (PR) — two types
Graham Steell murmur: high-pitched, early diastolic murmur at the LUSB caused by functional PR in pulmonary hypertension. The pulmonary artery and PV annulus dilate from high PA pressure → PV leaflets can no longer coapt → PR. Heard in severe MS with pulmonary hypertension, Eisenmenger syndrome, IPAH. Increases on inspiration (more RV filling). Organic PR (post-surgical, congenital): lower-pitched than Graham Steell murmur because PA pressure is low → lower pressure gradient driving regurgitation → lower-pitched murmur (may be difficult to hear). Common after TOF repair.

## Mid-diastolic murmurs — low-pitched rumbles

Sign: Mitral stenosis — mid-diastolic rumble
Timing: begins after the opening snap (early-mid diastole), decrescendo, with presystolic accentuation (in sinus rhythm — atrial contraction forces more flow through the stenotic MV → murmur loudest just before S1). In AF: presystolic accentuation is ABSENT. Pitch: low-pitched (like a rumble or thunder) — BELL with very light pressure, patient in left lateral decubitus. Location: strictly localised to the apex — does NOT radiate. If you move the stethoscope even 1–2 cm from the apex, the rumble disappears. This localisation is itself a diagnostic feature. How to bring out the rumble: ask the patient to exercise briefly (5–10 sit-ups, or have them roll to the left lateral decubitus) → increased cardiac output → more flow through the MV → louder rumble. This is especially useful in mild MS where the rumble may be nearly silent at rest.

Sign: Austin Flint murmur
A low-pitched, mid-diastolic rumble at the apex in the presence of severe AR — without any structural mitral valve disease. Mechanism: the large AR jet bounces off the anterior mitral leaflet and forces it partially shut in mid-diastole, creating functional partial mitral obstruction → turbulent flow through the semi-occluded MV → rumble. Distinguishing from MS: Austin Flint murmur has no opening snap (the MV leaflets are normal, no snap); no loud S1; the AR murmur and signs of wide pulse pressure are present; echo shows no structural MS. The Austin Flint murmur is softer and less harsh than true MS rumble, and disappears when AR is surgically corrected.

Sign: Carey Coombs murmur
A soft, short mid-diastolic rumble at the apex during acute rheumatic fever with active carditis. Caused by thickening and oedema of the MV leaflets (not yet fixed stenosis) + increased flow across the inflamed MV from the accompanying functional MR. Not fixed — disappears as acute inflammation resolves. Distinguishes from established MS: no fixed opening snap, associated with evidence of acute rheumatic fever (arthritis, fever, elevated ESR/CRP, skin manifestations). Indonesian relevance: rheumatic fever remains common in Indonesian children — the Carey Coombs murmur may be the first cardiac sign of what will become rheumatic MS.

Sign: Tricuspid stenosis (TS) — mid-diastolic murmur
Rare in isolation; almost always accompanies MS in rheumatic heart disease. Low-pitched diastolic murmur at the lower left sternal border (not the apex). Increases on inspiration (Rivero-Carvalho — more flow across the TV on inspiration). Associated with: giant a waves in the JVP (RA contracting against the obstructed TV), prominent a wave presystolic accentuation (in sinus rhythm), elevated JVP, hepatomegaly, ascites.

## Continuous murmurs

Cause | Character | Location | Key features
PDA (patent ductus arteriosus) | Continuous, "machinery" or "Gibson" murmur — crescendo to S2, then decrescendo through diastole. Never completely silent. | Upper left sternal border / left infraclavicular area | Wide pulse pressure; bounding pulses; thrill often palpable. In Eisenmenger PDA: murmur shortens or disappears (equalization of pressures); differential cyanosis (lower limbs more cyanosed than upper limbs — right-to-left ductal shunting bypasses only the lower aorta).
Coronary AV fistula | Continuous murmur | Variable (depends on fistula location) | Rare; confirmed by coronary angiography
Venous hum | Continuous, low-pitched humming; louder in diastole; abolished by firm pressure on the jugular vein or turning the head | Infraclavicular / supraclavicular area | Innocent finding — the only truly innocent continuous murmur. Normal in children and young adults. Abolishing it with neck pressure confirms it is venous.
Mammary souffle | Continuous or systolic murmur over the breast | Breast area bilaterally | Normal in pregnancy and lactation — increased blood flow through the breast vasculature. Disappears post-partum.

Exam tip: Diastolic murmur mnemonics:
Early diastolic (immediately after S2, high-pitched, decrescendo): AR, PR
Mid-diastolic (after OS or in mid-diastole, low-pitched, rumbling): MS, TS, Austin Flint (functional from AR), Carey Coombs (rheumatic carditis)
Presystolic accentuation (end of diastole, just before S1): MS in sinus rhythm, TS in sinus rhythm
All diastolic murmurs are pathological in adults. Never reassure a patient with an adult diastolic murmur without echocardiographic confirmation.
sections.title: Study text

sections.body:
Before reading a single waveform, you must understand what the ECG is actually recording. Everything else — every pattern, every abnormality — follows from this single physical concept.

## The ECG records electrical vectors

The ECG does not directly image the heart or measure blood pressure. It measures voltage differences between skin electrodes, sampled at high frequency over time. These voltage differences are caused by the electrical currents that flow through the body as waves of depolarisation and repolarisation spread across cardiac muscle.

The key word is vector. At each instant in the cardiac cycle, the net electrical activity of the entire heart can be represented as a single arrow — pointing in the direction the dominant electrical wavefront is travelling, with a magnitude proportional to the amount of tissue being activated. The ECG draws that arrow's projection onto each lead, over time.

Key concept: Toward the positive electrode = upward deflection. Away = downward. Perpendicular = flat.
This single rule explains every waveform in every lead. When ventricular depolarisation (QRS) spreads from right to left and downward — toward the apex — it produces a positive (upward) deflection in leads that face the apex (II, V5, V6) and a negative (downward) deflection in leads that face away (aVR). You do not need to memorise which leads have positive or negative deflections — you can reason them from the vector direction.

## Depolarisation vs repolarisation — and why they look different

The cardiac electrical cycle has two phases:

- Depolarisation — the electrical wave that triggers contraction. Positive charge flows into cells. This is a rapid, organised process.
- Repolarisation — the return of cells to resting potential. Charge flows back out. This is slower and more spread out.

Here is the key insight most students miss: in the ventricles, depolarisation spreads from endocardium to epicardium, but repolarisation spreads from epicardium to endocardium — in the opposite direction. Because repolarisation moves in the opposite direction to depolarisation, its vector also reverses. This is why, despite being an opposite electrical event, the T wave is normally in the same direction as the QRS in most leads — the two opposite vectors partially cancel each other's direction.

Key concept: Normal T wave points the same way as the QRS because repolarisation runs backwards
Depolarisation: endocardium → epicardium. Repolarisation: epicardium → endocardium. Since the ECG records direction, and repolarisation runs "backwards," its net vector actually points in the same overall direction as the QRS vector. When T waves are opposite to the QRS (T-wave inversion), this reversal of normal is an abnormal finding — it means repolarisation is abnormal (ischaemia, bundle branch block, strain, metabolic).

## Why the ECG grid matters

The ECG paper is a standardised grid. Every single measurement you make depends on knowing what the squares mean. Commit these four numbers to memory:

Diagram: ECG paper grid — the two values you must know before reading any tracing (drawing not carried over)

These four values are used in every single calculation you do on an ECG — rate, PR interval, QRS duration, QTc. Not knowing them means every interval measurement is guesswork.

Mental model: Think of the ECG lead as a camera watching a moving crowd. Each person walking toward the camera shows as a positive signal. Each person walking away shows as negative. The size of the signal tells you how many people are walking. The width tells you how long it takes the crowd to pass. Every ECG finding is a statement about direction, magnitude, and timing of the cardiac electrical "crowd."

## Dipoles and the resting potential

In resting muscle, the inside of every cell is negatively charged (about −90 mV) relative to the outside. This makes the cell surface appear uniformly positive. When depolarisation begins, the charge reverses locally — inside becomes positive, outside becomes negative. This creates a dipole: a positive charge in front (depolarised tissue) and a negative charge behind (still resting tissue).

The ECG electrode detects the leading positive charge of the depolarisation wavefront. When this wavefront moves toward an electrode → positive deflection. When it moves away → negative deflection. When it has passed (all tissue depolarised, no wavefront) → no signal. This is why the isoelectric line exists between the P wave and QRS — all atrial tissue is depolarised and waiting for the ventricles.

Exam tip: This explains why pericarditis and ischaemia displace the ST segment differently. In STEMI, the injured zone loses its resting potential — there is a constant "injury current" flowing from normal to injured myocardium at rest. This makes the baseline appear elevated in the leads facing the injury, not the ST segment elevated. In reality, it is the TP segment (true baseline) that is depressed, making the ST segment appear elevated. Understanding this resolves the "why is there ST elevation?" question from first principles.

Checkpoint: Lead aVR consistently shows a negative (downward) QRS complex in normal patients. Using the vector rule, why?
The normal ventricular depolarisation vector points leftward and downward toward the LV apex. Lead aVR's positive electrode is on the right shoulder — pointing toward the upper right. The main depolarisation vector is moving away from aVR's positive electrode → the QRS deflects downward (negative) in aVR. This is normal. Any positive QRS in aVR means the electrical axis is pointing toward the upper right — extreme axis deviation, ventricular tachycardia, or lead reversal.
sections.title: Study text

sections.body:
Time is muscle. Every minute of STEMI is another 2 million cardiomyocytes dying. Speed comes from pattern recognition so automatic that the cath lab call is in progress before you've finished reading the ECG.

## The diagnostic criteria

STEMI is diagnosed when all three criteria are met:

1. Symptoms consistent with ACS (chest pain, dyspnoea, jaw/arm pain, diaphoresis, epigastric discomfort — or any unexplained haemodynamic instability in patients who may not feel pain, e.g., diabetics, women, elderly)
2. ECG changes — ST elevation at the J-point in ≥2 contiguous leads: ≥2 mm in V2–V3 (≥1.5 mm in women, ≥2.5 mm in men under 40) or ≥1 mm in other leads OR new LBBB (in symptomatic patients)
3. Elevated biomarkers — but do NOT wait for troponin results before treatment. Treat on ECG + symptoms alone.

Key concept: Do not wait for troponins. Treat STEMI on ECG + clinical presentation.
Troponin I and T take 3–6 hours to rise above the 99th percentile detection limit. Waiting for a troponin result before activating the cath lab delays reperfusion by hours. The STEMI ECG + clinical presentation is sufficient for immediate PCI activation. Troponin will subsequently confirm the diagnosis. This is the meaning of "door-to-balloon time ≤90 minutes" — the clock starts when the patient arrives, not when the troponin returns.

## Territory mapping — artery from leads in 10 seconds

ECG pattern | Territory | Likely artery | Specific watch-outs
ST↑ II, III, aVF | Inferior | RCA (~85%) or LCx (~15%) | Get V4R (RV involvement), check for AV block, never give nitrates until V4R cleared
III > II elevation | Inferior, likely RCA proximal | RCA | High RV infarction risk
II > III elevation | Inferior, possibly LCx | LCx | May miss if only standard leads checked
ST↑ V1–V4 | Anterior | LAD | Large territory → high HF risk. Get echo urgently. Consider cardiogenic shock.
ST↑ V1–V6 + I + aVL | Extensive anterior | Proximal LAD | "Widow-maker." Highest mortality. Cardiogenic shock likely.
ST↑ V5–V6 + I + aVL | Lateral | LCx or LAD diagonal | Check for posterior involvement (V7–V9)
ST↑ aVR > V1 + diffuse ST↓ | Left main or 3-vessel | LMCA or proximal LAD | Highest risk pattern. CABG may be preferred over PCI.
ST↓ V1–V3 + tall R V1 | Posterior | RCA or LCx | Get posterior leads V7–V9. Often missed as "NSTEMI."
ST↑ V4R ≥1 mm | RV | Proximal RCA | Preload-dependent. IV fluids. No nitrates, diuretics, morphine.

## Reciprocal ST depression

Reciprocal changes are mirror-image ST depressions in leads geometrically opposite to the zone of ST elevation. They occur because the same injury current that elevates ST in the facing leads depresses it in the opposite leads. Reciprocal changes:

- Confirm STEMI — their presence strongly supports the diagnosis and argues against benign ST elevation variants.
- Indicate severity — more leads with reciprocal change = larger territory = higher risk.
- Guide territory — reciprocal changes in I/aVL alongside inferior STEMI confirm RCA (inferior elevation + lateral reciprocal depression). Absence of this pattern suggests LCx (which may not produce prominent lateral reciprocal change).

## The STEMI management pathway

The principles are simple even if the pathway seems complex:

1. Identify the STEMI (ECG + symptoms)
2. Activate the cath lab immediately — "STEMI call"
3. Dual antiplatelet therapy: aspirin 300 mg + P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor 180 mg loading preferred, or prasugrel if not prior stroke)
4. Anticoagulation: IV UFH or bivalirudin
5. Primary PCI ≤90 minutes from first medical contact (FMC-to-balloon). If primary PCI not available within 120 minutes of FMC → thrombolysis within 30 minutes of arrival (fibrinolysis is time-sensitive — most benefit within 3 hours of symptom onset)
6. Post-PCI: DAPT × 12 months minimum, ACEi, statin, beta-blocker, cardiac rehab

Clinical link: The inferior STEMI + hypotension after nitrates scenario is one of the most tested clinical decisions in cardiology. The sequence: inferior STEMI identified → physician gives GTN spray (reflex, without thinking) → patient collapses with BP 70 mmHg → GTN has caused venodilation → RV infarction (preload-dependent) has no preload left → cardiac output crashes. Every physician must automatically check V4R before giving nitrates in inferior STEMI. If V4R shows ST elevation, the only intervention is IV saline boluses and urgent PCI — no GTN, no morphine, no diuretics.

Exam tip: The ECG evolution after successful reperfusion: ST elevation begins to fall within 30–60 minutes of successful PCI
"Reperfusion arrhythmias" may occur (accelerated idioventricular rhythm — AIVR — is a classic marker of successful reperfusion, not dangerous, do not treat)
T waves invert over 24–72 hours (reperfusion T waves)
Q waves may develop even after successful reperfusion — they mark infarcted (not viable) myocardium
Persistent ST elevation >3 months after MI suggests LV aneurysm (scar tissue bulges during systole)

Checkpoint: A patient arrives with 3 hours of crushing chest pain. ECG: ST elevation 3 mm in V1–V5, ST depression in II, III, aVF. HR 110, BP 90/65. What is the diagnosis, the immediate management, and the haemodynamic reason for concern?
Extensive anterior STEMI (V1–V5) with inferior reciprocal ST depression — almost certainly proximal LAD occlusion ("widow-maker"). Haemodynamic concern: BP 90/65 and HR 110 with anterior ST elevation indicates the large LV territory is already compromised — cardiogenic shock or impending shock from pump failure of a large anterior wall. Immediate management: (1) Activate cath lab urgently (primary PCI <90 min). (2) Aspirin 300 mg + ticagrelor 180 mg. (3) IV heparin. (4) Do not give large fluid bolus (congested lungs, not hypovolaemia). (5) Consider early MCS — Impella or IABP — for haemodynamic support peri-PCI. (6) Vasopressors/inotropes if BP continues to fall (norepinephrine first, add dobutamine if needed). Post-PCI: urgent echo to assess EF and wall motion. This patient will likely need GDMT optimisation and may need ICD discussion at 90-day reassessment.
sections.title: Study text

sections.body:
Some of the deadliest ECG patterns don't meet classic STEMI criteria but require the same urgency. And some patterns look like STEMI but are not ischaemic at all. Recognising both saves lives.

## STEMI equivalents — urgent PCI without classic criteria

### Wellens' Syndrome

Wellens' syndrome represents a critical proximal LAD stenosis that has recently had a transient occlusion, now reperfused. The patient is pain-free or has resolved pain, troponin may be mildly elevated or near-normal, but the ECG shows characteristic reperfusion T-wave changes in V2–V3 that signal imminent massive anterior STEMI.

Two patterns:

- Type A (biphasic): Biphasic T wave in V2–V3 — positive initial deflection, then negative. More common.
- Type B (symmetric deep inversion): Deep, symmetric T-wave inversions in V2–V3. Less common but equally dangerous.

Warning: Do NOT exercise-test a patient with Wellens' syndrome. The exercise-induced rise in HR and O₂ demand will re-occlude the critical LAD lesion. The patient needs urgent coronary angiography and revascularisation as an inpatient. Many have undergone exercise testing because the pain had resolved and the troponin was minimal — and suffered massive anterior MI on the treadmill. This is one of the most important ECG-safety rules in clinical practice.

### De Winter T waves

De Winter pattern is an STEMI equivalent caused by proximal LAD occlusion where the classic ST elevation fails to develop. Instead, a unique pattern appears:

- Upsloping ST depression at the J-point in V1–V6, followed by tall, symmetric, positive T waves (the ST depression "slopes up" into a tall T) — producing a pattern that looks like an inverted STEMIs.
- ST elevation in aVR (1–2 mm).
- QRS may be normal width.

The mechanism: the ischaemic subendocardium produces upsloping ST depression, but the hyperacute T waves of impending occlusion superimpose — creating this characteristic pointed T with depressed ST. Treat as proximal LAD STEMI — urgent cath lab activation.

### Left Main / aVR elevation pattern

Described in Chapter 10: ST elevation in aVR >V1 with diffuse ST depression in all other leads = left main occlusion or proximal LAD. This patient is the highest-risk ACS presentation. Often presents with cardiogenic shock. Likely needs emergency CABG rather than PCI if multivessel disease confirmed. Do not delay angiography.

### Sgarbossa criteria — STEMI in LBBB

LBBB distorts the ST segment so severely that ischaemia changes are masked in most leads. However, three specific criteria can detect STEMI in the setting of LBBB or paced rhythms:

Criterion | Threshold | Specificity
1. ST elevation ≥1 mm in a lead with a positive (upward) QRS | ≥1 mm concordant ST elevation | High specificity (94%), lower sensitivity
2. ST depression ≥1 mm in V1, V2, or V3 | ≥1 mm concordant ST depression | High specificity (96%)
3. ST elevation ≥5 mm in a lead with a negative (downward) QRS | ≥5 mm discordant ST elevation | Moderate — use modified criterion (ST/S ratio >0.25)

The modified Sgarbossa criteria (Smith) use a ratio: if the absolute ST elevation in any lead divided by the depth of the S wave (or QRS) is ≥0.25, it indicates occlusion MI. This is more sensitive than the original absolute 5 mm threshold.

Key concept: In LBBB: concordant ST changes (same direction as QRS) are abnormal and indicate STEMI
In LBBB, the ST segment is expected to be discordant — opposite to the QRS direction. In leads with a positive QRS, ST should be depressed. In leads with a negative QRS, ST should be elevated. When you see ST changes that are concordant (same direction as the QRS), this reversal of the expected pattern signals acute injury current overriding the LBBB pattern. Concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm in leads with positive QRS = STEMI until proven otherwise.

## STEMI mimics — elevated ST that is NOT ischaemia

ST elevation occurs in many non-ischaemic conditions. Recognising these prevents unnecessary cath lab activation while ensuring genuine STEMIs are not missed.

### Pericarditis

Distinguishing features from STEMI:

- ST elevation is concave-up (like a smile) in pericarditis vs convex-up or flat (tombstone) in STEMI
- ST elevation is diffuse — present in many leads across different territories simultaneously (I, II, aVF, V2–V6 all elevated = cannot represent one coronary territory)
- PR depression — almost pathognomonic of pericarditis. Inflammation of the atrial myocardium depresses the PR segment (atrial injury current). Best seen in II and V5.
- No reciprocal changes (except aVR, which shows ST elevation opposite to the diffuse elevation in other leads)
- Spodick's sign: downward sloping of the TP segment in limb leads (a useful sign of acute pericarditis)

### Early repolarisation

Common benign variant, especially in young athletic men. Features:

- ST elevation, typically in V2–V5 and/or inferior leads, often with a "fishhook" or "notch" at the J-point
- Concave-up ("happy face") ST morphology
- Prominent T waves, often tall
- Present on multiple previous ECGs (a stable finding)
- No symptoms, no biomarker elevation

Caution: "Malignant early repolarisation" — early repolarisation in the inferior and lateral leads (not just anterior) in the setting of syncope or resuscitated VF may actually be a risk factor for idiopathic VF. This is rare but important — not all early repolarisation is benign.

### Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH)

LVH produces a "strain pattern" in V5–V6 and I/aVL — downsloping ST depression + T-wave inversion (secondary repolarisation change). In V1–V2, reciprocal ST elevation may occur. This can mimic posterior MI. Clue: the ST elevation in V1–V2 is concave-up and accompanied by classic LVH voltage criteria (Sokolow-Lyon: S in V1 + R in V5 or V6 >35 mm; or Cornell: R in aVL + S in V3 >28 mm in men, >20 mm in women).

### Brugada pattern

Coved ST elevation in V1–V2 (Type 1 Brugada) — a specific morphology of ST elevation (convex-up, descending into an inverted T wave) that does not represent ischaemia. See Chapter 15 for full detail. Key: no chest pain, normal coronaries, family history of sudden death.

### Osborn waves (J waves)

Positive notch at the J-point (end of QRS), most prominent in V3–V6 and inferior leads. Seen in hypothermia (most classic — body temperature <30°C), hypercalcaemia, and sometimes in early repolarisation or Brugada. The waves are characteristic of hypothermia — their presence in a patient with altered consciousness and cold skin confirms the diagnosis.

### Benign vs pathological — the 4-point checklist

Exam tip: Before treating a "STEMI," quickly check these 4 points: 1. Symptoms? ST elevation without chest pain/equivalent → think non-ischaemic (pericarditis, early repolarisation). STEMI without pain is possible (diabetics, women, elderly) but less common.
2. Morphology? Concave (smile) → likely benign/pericarditis. Convex (tombstone/flat top) → worry for STEMI.
3. Territory? Multi-territory elevation (diffuse) → pericarditis or global hypoxic injury. Single-territory elevation (inferior alone, anterior alone) → STEMI.
4. PR depression? PR depression → pericarditis. Hyperacute T waves → early STEMI.
If in doubt and the patient has symptoms → treat as STEMI. A negative angiogram is much safer than a missed STEMI.

Checkpoint: A 28-year-old man presents with sharp pleuritic chest pain, worse lying flat, better sitting forward. ECG: PR depression in leads II, V4–V6. ST elevation in I, II, aVF, V2–V6 — all concave upward. No reciprocal changes except aVR. Temperature 37.8°C, mild pericardial friction rub on auscultation. What is the diagnosis, and what confirms this is NOT a STEMI?
Acute pericarditis. Confirmed against STEMI by: (1) Pleuritic pain, positional (better sitting forward = pericardial friction reduces) — ACS pain is not positional; (2) Concave ST elevation in a diffuse distribution across multiple territories (inferior + anterior + lateral) — no single coronary can produce all of these simultaneously; (3) PR depression — classic for pericarditis, does not occur in STEMI; (4) No reciprocal ST depression (except aVR which shows minimal elevation); (5) Friction rub on auscultation; (6) Young healthy man with febrile illness (viral pericarditis context). Treatment: NSAIDs (ibuprofen 600 mg TDS or aspirin 750–1000 mg TDS) + colchicine 0.5 mg BD for 3 months (prevents recurrence). Restrict strenuous activity for 3 months.

sections.body:
The cardiac axis tells you the dominant direction of ventricular depolarisation. In 30 seconds, using only leads I and aVF, you can classify the axis as normal, left deviated, right deviated, or extreme — and each deviation narrows a clinical differential.

## What axis means

The QRS axis is the direction of the dominant ventricular depolarisation vector in the frontal plane, measured in degrees from the positive pole of lead I (defined as 0°). It reflects where the bulk of the LV muscle mass is activated and in what direction.

Normal axis: −30° to +90°. This corresponds to the direction one would expect the LV vector to point — generally downward and leftward, toward the apex.

## The two-lead quick method

You only need leads I and aVF for the initial classification:

Lead I (0°) | Lead aVF (90°) | Axis | Degrees
Positive (upward) | Positive (upward) | Normal axis | 0° to +90°
Positive (upward) | Negative (downward) | Left axis deviation (LAD) | 0° to −90°
Negative (downward) | Positive (upward) | Right axis deviation (RAD) | +90° to +180°
Negative (downward) | Negative (downward) | Extreme axis deviation | −90° to ±180°

Key concept: Both positive (I ↑ and aVF ↑) = normal. One negative = deviated away from that lead.
The trick: lead I points to the left (0°). Lead aVF points down (90°). If the cardiac vector is in the normal range (between 0° and 90°), it is moving toward both lead I and lead aVF → both positive. If it deviates left (e.g., −60°), it is still toward lead I but now away from aVF → I positive, aVF negative = LAD. If it deviates right, it moves away from lead I → I negative, aVF positive = RAD. Both negative = extreme deviation — the vector is pointing up and to the right, away from both leads.

## Left axis deviation (LAD) — causes

- Left anterior fascicular block (LAFB) — most common cause. Axis −45° to −90°.
- Inferior MI — the inferior wall (which contributes a downward/inferior vector) is necrotic. Net vector shifts superiorly (left) because the inferior vector is missing.
- LVH — the enlarged LV mass rotates the axis leftward.
- Pre-excitation (WPW) — the delta wave activates the ventricle in an abnormal direction, depending on the accessory pathway location.
- Ostium primum ASD — a congenital defect associated with characteristic LAD in the context of right heart enlargement (an unusual combination).
- Pacemaker rhythm — depends on pacing lead location.
- Normal variant in obesity — horizontal heart position shifts axis leftward.

Clinical link: The most common cause of significant left axis deviation (−45° or more) on cardiology exams is LAFB. When you see this combination — wide QRS with left axis deviation — think bifascicular block first (RBBB + LAFB). Confirm RBBB with rSR' in V1 and wide S in lead I.

## Right axis deviation (RAD) — causes

- Normal in tall, thin adults and children — the vertical heart position shifts the axis rightward.
- RVH — enlarged RV mass dominates and rotates the vector rightward and anteriorly.
- Pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonale — RVH pattern develops with chronic RV pressure overload.
- Massive PE — acute RV pressure overload shifts axis rightward (S1Q3T3 pattern — see below).
- Left posterior fascicular block (LPFB) — axis +90° to +120°, after excluding RVH.
- Lateral MI — the lateral LV wall vector is lost, net vector shifts rightward (away from the infarct).
- RBBB — the terminal QRS forces are directed rightward and anteriorly (toward the right bundle's territory).
- Left-right arm lead reversal — lead I inverts → negative in I → appears as RAD.

Exam tip: S1Q3T3 pattern of pulmonary embolism: S wave in lead I + Q wave in lead III + T-wave inversion in lead III. This is a right heart strain pattern, not specific to PE — the full right heart strain picture includes: S1Q3T3, RAD, RBBB or RBBB-like morphology, sinus tachycardia, T-wave inversions in V1–V4, and occasionally PR prolongation. The pattern occurs in only 20–25% of PE cases — its absence does not exclude PE. Sinus tachycardia alone is the most common ECG finding in PE. The primary value of the right heart strain pattern when present is to increase clinical suspicion in the right context.

## Extreme axis deviation

Axis between −90° and ±180°: both lead I and aVF are negative. Causes:

- Ventricular tachycardia — an ectopic ventricular focus firing from an unusual location
- WPW with antidromic tachycardia
- Hyperkalaemia — profound conduction disease
- Right ventricular pacemaker (apical pacing produces extreme LAD)
- Lead reversal — limb lead placement errors

Checkpoint: ECG: Lead I shows a predominantly negative QRS. Lead aVF shows a predominantly positive QRS. There is no bundle branch block pattern and the QRS is narrow at 95 ms. What is the axis, and what are the two most common causes in an adult?
Lead I negative + aVF positive = right axis deviation. QRS narrow (95 ms) rules out BBB as the cause of RAD. In an adult without acute illness, the two most common causes are: (1) RVH from pulmonary disease or pulmonary hypertension — the enlarged RV dominates the frontal vector. Look for tall R in V1, right atrial enlargement (peaked P in II), and T-wave inversions V1–V3. (2) Normal variant in a tall, thin individual — vertical heart position. In the context of acute chest pain and dyspnoea, right heart strain from massive PE must also be considered immediately.

sections.body:
Enlarged chambers leave ECG signatures. Most are subtle and require systematic measurement, but some — like RVH with right axis deviation and the P-mitrale of severe MS — are diagnostically powerful when recognised quickly.

## Atrial enlargement

Atrial size is best assessed on P-wave morphology in lead II and V1. Normal P wave: <120 ms wide (3 small squares), <2.5 mm tall (2.5 small squares).

### Right atrial enlargement (RAE) — "P-pulmonale"

- Tall, peaked P waves in II, III, aVF ≥2.5 mm
- Biphasic P in V1 with prominent positive initial deflection (>1.5 mm tall)
- P wave may be narrow (duration normal) but tall

Causes: pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary stenosis. The "P" in P-pulmonale helps remember the pulmonary associations.

### Left atrial enlargement (LAE) — "P-mitrale"

- Broad, notched P wave ("M-shaped") in lead II ≥120 ms
- The two humps represent right and left atrial depolarisation — the notch between them widens when LA activation is delayed
- Biphasic P in V1 with prominent negative terminal component (>1 mm deep, >1 mm wide — wider than 1 small square)

Causes: mitral stenosis (most classic), LV dysfunction (raised LA pressure), hypertension, AF predisposition (LAE precedes AF development).

Key concept: P-mitrale in II (broad, notched, ≥120 ms) + biphasic P in V1 (prominent negative terminal) = LAE
The negative terminal component of the P in V1 represents the LA depolarisation vector moving posteriorly and leftward — away from V1. When the LA is enlarged, this posterior deflection is deeper and wider. Measuring the negative terminal component of P in V1: if it is >1 mm deep AND >1 mm wide (i.e., >1 small square area), this is significant LAE. This criterion is more sensitive than the broad P in II alone.

## Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH)

The enlarged LV produces taller-than-normal R waves in left-facing leads (V5–V6, I, aVL) and deeper-than-normal S waves in right-facing leads (V1, V2). Multiple voltage criteria exist:

### Common voltage criteria:

- Sokolow-Lyon: S in V1 + R in V5 or V6 >35 mm. Sensitivity ~50%, specificity ~85%.
- Cornell: R in aVL + S in V3 >28 mm (men) or >20 mm (women). Slightly better sensitivity.
- R wave in aVL ≥12 mm alone — simple, reasonably specific.
- R in V5 or V6 ≥26 mm alone.

Clinical link: Voltage criteria alone have poor sensitivity (often <50% for LVH confirmed on echo). A tall person with thin chest wall may have high voltages without LVH. A person with obesity, COPD, or pericardial effusion may have LVH without meeting voltage criteria. The ECG diagnosis of LVH is strengthened by accompanying features: LAE (widened P in II), left axis deviation, LV strain pattern (downsloping ST depression + T inversion in I, aVL, V5–V6). Cornell criteria + strain pattern together have better diagnostic accuracy than voltage alone.

### LV strain pattern

The "strain" pattern refers to the repolarisation changes that accompany pressure-overload LVH (as in hypertension or aortic stenosis):

- Downsloping ST depression in I, aVL, V5–V6
- Asymmetric T-wave inversion in V5–V6 (the T wave has a gradual upslope and abrupt downslope)
- In right-facing leads (V1–V2), reciprocal ST elevation may be seen

This pattern mirrors LV repolarisation abnormality from sustained pressure overload. It does not represent acute ischaemia but suggests long-standing hypertension and increases the probability of future cardiac events.

## Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)

The enlarged RV dominates the electrical forces, shifting them rightward and anteriorly (toward V1).

- Right axis deviation (>+90°)
- Tall R wave in V1 (R > S in V1, or R > 7 mm) — the RV vector now dominates anteriorly
- Persistent S waves in V5–V6 — the RV vector moves away from left-facing leads
- T-wave inversions in V1–V3 (secondary repolarisation change, RV strain)
- RAE (P-pulmonale) — often present in the same conditions that cause RVH

Exam tip: RVH vs posterior MI vs RBBB in V1 — the three causes of tall R in V1: RVH: RAD + tall R in V1 + T inversion V1–V3 + P-pulmonale. No broad R (R is narrow). Clinical context: pulmonary hypertension, congenital heart disease.
Posterior MI: Tall, broad R in V1 (mirror of Q wave) + ST depression in V1–V3 + upright T waves in V1–V3 (mirror of posterior T inversion). Clinical context: chest pain, RCA/LCx territory.
RBBB: QRS ≥120 ms, rSR' in V1, wide S in I/V5–V6. The terminal R' is broad. Clinical context: any.

Checkpoint: An ECG shows P waves >120 ms wide with notching in lead II, and a biphasic P in V1 with negative terminal component 1.5 mm deep and 1.5 mm wide. QRS voltage in aVL R wave = 14 mm. What is the combined interpretation?
Two findings: (1) Left atrial enlargement — broad notched P ≥120 ms in II (P-mitrale) + biphasic P in V1 with negative terminal >1 mm × 1 mm. (2) LVH — R in aVL ≥12 mm (criterion met at 14 mm). Together, this picture suggests longstanding pressure or volume overload of the left heart — most likely chronic hypertension or mitral stenosis. In hypertension: LA enlarges first (raised LA pressure from stiff LV), then LVH develops. In mitral stenosis: LA enlarges from obstruction, but the LV is often spared (LA to LV flow is restricted). If there is associated strain pattern (downsloping ST depression + T inversion in V5–V6), this favours hypertension with LVH strain. The combination is a "score" — echo is needed for definitive assessment.
