sections.body:
Not all cardiomyopathies are treated the same. Amyloid requires a drug that is completely wrong for ischaemic CMP. HCM is managed the opposite way to dilated CMP. ARVC has a different sudden death risk profile. This chapter covers the key entities where the specific diagnosis changes the management.

## Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)

HCM is the most common inherited cardiomyopathy (1 in 500), caused by mutations in sarcomere protein genes (MYH7, MYBPC3 most common). Characterised by asymmetric LVH (usually septal) without a secondary cause (not from HTN or AS).

### Haemodynamic problem

In ~70% of HCM patients: the hypertrophied septum creates dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO) — the basal septum bulges into the LVOTO during systole, and systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the anterior mitral leaflet worsens the obstruction. Result: pressure gradient across the LVOTO, impaired LV emptying, MR (from SAM pulling the MV toward the septum), and diastolic dysfunction from the stiff, non-compliant hypertrophied LV.

### What worsens LVOTO — the management axis

Worsens LVOTO (avoid): • Reduced preload (dehydration, nitrates, diuretics, Valsalva, standing) — less LV volume → septum more obstructive relative to LV size
• Reduced afterload (vasodilators, DHP-CCBs, ACEi) — further reduces SVR → reflex tachycardia + worsens obstruction
• Increased contractility (inotropes, digoxin, dobutamine) — more forceful contraction worsens SAM
• Tachycardia — shorter diastolic fill time → smaller LV volume → worse obstruction

Improves LVOTO (use): • Increased preload (squatting, passive leg raise, IV fluids) — larger LV volume → septum less obstructive
• Increased afterload (handgrip exercise, phenylephrine) — higher SVR without increasing HR
• Reduced contractility (beta-blockers, non-DHP CCBs, disopyramide, mavacamten) — less force → less SAM
• Bradycardia — longer diastole → better LV filling → larger LV volume → less obstruction

Key concept: In obstructive HCM, the drugs that save patients with HFrEF can kill — and vice versa
This is the most testable HCM fact. Digoxin (positive inotrope — worsens LVOTO), nitrates (preload reduction — worsens LVOTO), DHP calcium channel blockers (nifedipine, amlodipine — vasodilate without rate control → reflex tachycardia → worsens LVOTO), and ACEi/ARB (after-load reduction → worsens LVOTO) are all dangerous in obstructive HCM. Dobutamine is absolutely contraindicated. Management: beta-blockers first-line, then non-DHP CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem), then disopyramide (adds negative inotropy), then mavacamten (myosin inhibitor — first disease-modifying drug in HCM, EXPLORER-HCM trial), then septal reduction therapy (alcohol septal ablation or surgical myectomy).

### HCM and sudden cardiac death

HCM is the most common cause of SCD in young athletes. Risk stratification uses the HCM Risk-SCD calculator (ESC) incorporating: max LV wall thickness, family history of SCD, unexplained syncope, non-sustained VT, LA diameter, LVOTO gradient, age. Score ≥6% at 5 years → ICD recommended. Score 4–6%: ICD considered. Score <4%: medical management.

Mavacamten (selective cardiac myosin inhibitor): EXPLORER-HCM trial — mavacamten significantly reduced LVOTO gradient, improved NYHA class, and improved exercise capacity in obstructive HCM. First disease-modifying therapy. Approved for symptomatic obstructive HCM on background BB or non-DHP CCB.

## Cardiac amyloidosis

Amyloid fibril deposits in the myocardium make the heart stiff and restrict filling. Two types:

- ATTR (transthyretin amyloid): misfolded transthyretin protein deposits. Two subtypes: wtATTR (wild-type, "senile amyloidosis" — male, >65 years, increasingly common cause of HFpEF) and vATTR (variant/hereditary — genetic mutation in TTR gene, younger onset, different ethnic distributions). Treated with tafamidis (stabilises TTR tetramer — ATTR-ACT trial: 30% mortality reduction).
- AL (light chain amyloid): clonal plasma cell dyscrasia deposits immunoglobulin light chains. Associated with multiple myeloma. Treated with chemotherapy (bortezomib-based, daratumumab). Worse prognosis than ATTR.

### ECG + Echo paradox — the classic teaching point

- ECG: low voltage limb leads (amyloid protein absorbs ECG signal) despite thick walls on echo — the "low voltage–LVH paradox." Pseudo-infarction Q waves (voltage attenuated in multiple leads mimics old MI)
- Echo: biventricular wall thickening, "granular sparkling" or "ground glass" appearance of myocardium (specific for amyloid on 2D echo), dilated atria, diastolic dysfunction, pericardial effusion, valve thickening
- CMR: diffuse global subendocardial LGE (unlike focal ischaemic LGE) — "can't null the myocardium" because amyloid infiltration is global. T1 mapping shows markedly elevated native T1 and ECV (extracellular volume) — amyloid occupies the extracellular space.
- Nuclear scintigraphy (Tc99m-DPD or PYP scan): bone tracer that preferentially binds ATTR amyloid — positive scan (grade 2/3 uptake) with negative serum/urine free light chains = ATTR confirmed without biopsy (high specificity).

Warning: Digoxin is dangerous in cardiac amyloidosis. Digoxin binds to amyloid fibrils in the myocardium → toxic accumulation → digoxin toxicity at serum levels that would be therapeutic in normal patients. Avoid digoxin in all amyloid cardiomyopathy. Also: ACEi/ARBs poorly tolerated in advanced amyloid (blood pressure is often low due to autonomic neuropathy — afterload reduction causes symptomatic hypotension). ICD: ATTR does not respond to ICD as reliably as ischaemic CMP — electromechanical dissociation (PEA) rather than VF is the mode of death in many amyloid patients, so ICD does not provide meaningful protection in advanced ATTR.

## Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC)

Genetic desmosome disease (PKP2, DSP, JUP mutations) causing fibro-fatty replacement of the RV free wall. Clinical features: ventricular arrhythmias (typically LBBB morphology VT from the RV), right heart failure in advanced disease, sudden cardiac death in young athletes. Epsilon waves on ECG (small notch after QRS in V1–V3), T-wave inversions V1–V4, RBBB morphology.

Management: ICD (high SCD risk), beta-blockers (antiarrhythmic), sotalol or amiodarone for VT control, avoid competitive sports (exercise dramatically worsens ARVC), catheter ablation for recurrent VT.

## Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) — genetic causes to know

DCM is the most common CMP — dilated LV, globally reduced EF, without a specific cause (or after excluding ischaemic, valvular, hypertensive causes). Genetic DCM is underappreciated:

- TTN (titin): most common genetic cause of DCM (~25% of familial DCM). Dilated LV, sometimes with peripartum exacerbation. CMR shows midwall LGE. Standard GDMT; genetic counselling for family members.
- LMNA (lamin A/C): dilated CMP + conduction disease (AV block, LBBB) + arrhythmias. High risk of sudden death even before EF falls to ICD threshold — ICD often recommended at EF ≤45% in confirmed LMNA mutation. Familial screening critical.
- Alcohol-related CMP: dose-dependent myocardial toxicity. Abstinence → partial or complete EF recovery in many patients. GDMT + strict abstinence.
- Anthracycline-induced CMP (cardiotoxicity from cancer chemotherapy — doxorubicin, epirubicin): type II toxicity — dose-dependent, partially reversible if caught early. Baseline echo before chemotherapy; monitoring during and after treatment. GDMT + ACEi/BB for cardioprotection.

Checkpoint: An 80-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea, bilateral ankle oedema, and carpal tunnel syndrome (bilateral, previously released surgically). Echo: concentric biventricular wall thickening, EF 48%, grade III diastolic dysfunction, pericardial effusion, "granular sparkling" appearance. ECG: low voltage in limb leads, QS pattern V1–V2 (no history of MI). What is the most likely diagnosis, how do you confirm it without biopsy, and what drug must you avoid?
Wild-type transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (wtATTR). The complete clinical picture: advanced age (wtATTR predominantly affects men over 65), carpal tunnel syndrome (TTR fibril deposits in the carpal tunnel — a classic extracardiac clue preceding cardiac involvement by years), echocardiographic infiltrative pattern (biventricular thickening, granular sparkling, diastolic dysfunction, pericardial effusion), ECG paradox (low voltage despite thickened walls + pseudo-infarct Q waves). Non-biopsy confirmation: Tc99m-DPD (or PYP) nuclear scintigraphy — grade 2/3 cardiac uptake + negative serum and urine free light chains = wtATTR confirmed with >99% specificity (excluding AL amyloid with the negative light chain assessment). This is the validated non-invasive diagnostic pathway. Drug to avoid: digoxin — binds amyloid fibrils → toxic accumulation at therapeutic levels → digoxin toxicity. Also avoid: ACEi/ARB if BP already low (common in amyloid due to autonomic dysfunction), diuretics should be used carefully (RV and LV filling pressure-sensitive). Treatment: tafamidis (if EF ≥40% — ATTR-ACT trial) — stabilises the TTR tetramer, slows amyloid deposition, reduces mortality and HF hospitalisation.

sections.body:
The average HF patient has five comorbidities. Each one interacts with HF in both directions — it worsens HF, and HF worsens it. Managing comorbidities correctly determines whether GDMT can actually be optimised or not.

## Atrial fibrillation (AF) — the most common arrhythmia in HF

AF and HF coexist in ~30–50% of patients and create a bidirectional vicious cycle:

- AF worsens HF: loss of atrial kick (10–20% of CO), tachycardia-mediated CMP if rate uncontrolled, irregular rhythm reduces LV filling efficiency
- HF causes AF: elevated filling pressures → LA dilation → atrial fibrosis → AF substrate; neurohormonal activation promotes AF

### Rate vs rhythm control in HF+AF

- Rate control target: resting HR <80 bpm (RACE II trial — strict <80 vs lenient <110: equivalent outcomes overall, but most cardiologists target <80 in symptomatic HF+AF). Drugs: beta-blockers (preferred in HFrEF — carvedilol, bisoprolol), digoxin (add-on or if BB not tolerated), amiodarone (if refractory — but thyroid/pulmonary/hepatic toxicity limit long-term use). Never diltiazem or verapamil in HFrEF.
- Rhythm control: EAST-AFNET 4 trial — early rhythm control significantly reduces cardiovascular outcomes vs usual care in patients with recently diagnosed AF, including those with HF. Catheter ablation for AF increasingly used in HFrEF: CASTLE-AF trial — AF ablation vs medical therapy in HFrEF+AF: significantly improved EF (+8%), reduced mortality and HF hospitalisation. The improvement was dramatic in patients who maintained sinus rhythm — some had complete recovery of EF suggesting tachycardia-mediated contribution to their HFrEF.
- Anticoagulation: HF alone is a risk factor for stroke in AF (contributes to the C in CHA₂DS₂-VASc — Congestive HF = 1 point). DOACs preferred over warfarin (ARISTOTLE, ENGAGE AF, ROCKET-AF: all showed non-inferiority or superiority to warfarin with less ICH).

## Renal dysfunction (CKD) — the cardiorenal syndrome

CKD and HF coexist in ~40–50% of patients. The cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) describes the bidirectional organ interactions:

- Type 1 CRS: acute worsening of cardiac function → acute kidney injury (ADHF → low CO → renal hypoperfusion + venous congestion → AKI)
- Type 2 CRS: chronic HF → chronic CKD (chronic reduced renal perfusion, neurohormonal activation → progressive nephrosclerosis)
- Type 3 CRS: acute kidney injury → acute cardiac injury (AKI → volume overload → acute HF)
- Type 4 CRS: chronic CKD → chronic cardiac dysfunction (hypertension from CKD, uraemic cardiomyopathy, calcified vessels)

Key concept: Worsening renal function during GDMT optimisation should not reflexively trigger drug cessation
ACEi, ARNi, and MRA all cause some degree of creatinine rise and GFR reduction from their desired mechanism (reducing intra-glomerular pressure). This is expected and generally safe. The ONTARGET and RALES post-hoc analyses, and the original CONSENSUS/SOLVD data, confirm that even patients with moderate CKD (eGFR 30–60) derive mortality benefit from ACEi. Stop or reduce the dose when: creatinine rises >30% from baseline, OR K⁺ exceeds 5.5 mmol/L, OR eGFR falls below 20 mL/min. Below these thresholds, do not automatically stop neurohormonal blockade — the creatinine rise is a side effect, not a contraindication. Discuss with nephrology for severe cases.

## Iron deficiency — the most undertreated comorbidity

Iron deficiency (ID) occurs in ~50% of HF patients (including those without anaemia) and is independently associated with reduced exercise capacity, worse QoL, and increased mortality. Iron is essential not just for haemoglobin but for mitochondrial function, oxidative phosphorylation, and myocardial energy production.

Definition in HF: ferritin <100 ng/mL, OR ferritin 100–299 ng/mL + TSAT <20%.

IV iron supplementation: AFFIRM-AHF, FAIR-HF2, IRONMAN trials — IV ferric carboxymaltose or ferric derisomaltose in HFrEF with ID:

- FAIR-HF (2009): IV iron vs saline in HFrEF+ID — significant improvement in NYHA class, 6-min walk distance, QoL. Even in non-anaemic patients.
- AFFIRM-AHF (2021): IV iron started during HF hospitalisation → significant reduction in recurrent HF hospitalisation at 52 weeks vs placebo.
- Oral iron does not work in HF (malabsorption from gut oedema, inflammatory state blocks absorption).
- Current recommendation (ESC 2021 Class IIa): IV ferric carboxymaltose for symptomatic HFrEF patients with ID to improve symptoms and reduce HF hospitalisation.

## Diabetes — SGLT2i changed everything

DM occurs in ~30–45% of HF patients and significantly worsens prognosis. The SGLT2 inhibitor era has been transformative: not only do SGLT2i treat both conditions simultaneously, they are among the safest glucose-lowering agents in HF (many other agents are problematic):

Drug class | Glucose lowering | HF impact
SGLT2i | Moderate | PREFERRED — reduces HF events, mortality, renal protection
Metformin | Moderate | Generally safe, may have mild CV benefit. Use cautiously in eGFR <30.
GLP-1 RA | Good | STEP-HFpEF (semaglutide) — benefits in obese HFpEF. Neutral in HFrEF (FIGHT, LIVE trials). Weight loss benefit may help HFpEF.
DPP-4 inhibitors | Mild | Saxagliptin: INCREASED HF hospitalisation (SAVOR-TIMI). Alogliptin: neutral but similar signal. Avoid saxagliptin in HF.
Thiazolidinediones (TZDs) | Good | CONTRAINDICATED in HF — cause fluid retention and worsen oedema. Rosiglitazone, pioglitazone. Avoid.
Insulin | Excellent | Causes Na/water retention at high doses. Use cautiously; prefer insulin regimens that minimise oedema risk.

## Anaemia

Anaemia (Hb <13 g/dL in men, <12 g/dL in women) occurs in ~30–50% of HF patients. Mechanisms: reduced erythropoiesis from CKD, iron deficiency, haemodilution, impaired BM from neurohormonal activation, RAAS inhibitors (ACEi/ARNi reduce EPO production slightly). Anaemia worsens HF by increasing cardiac demand (high-output demand on a failing heart). Management: identify and correct the cause — iron deficiency (most common, IV iron first), folate/B12 deficiency, EPO deficiency from CKD (ESA — erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, use with caution, target Hb 10–12 g/dL — higher targets worsen CV outcomes), treat underlying renal disease.

Checkpoint: A 68-year-old with HFrEF (EF 35%) and AF (HR 95 bpm on bisoprolol 5 mg OD) has ferritin 55 ng/mL (low), TSAT 15%, Hb 11.2 g/dL. His NYHA class has not improved beyond Class III despite optimal GDMT. What two additional interventions are evidence-based and should be pursued at this visit?
1. IV iron replacement — ferritin 55 ng/mL <100 ng/mL confirms iron deficiency (regardless of anaemia). AFFIRM-AHF and FAIR-HF data support IV ferric carboxymaltose (typically 1000 mg IV over 15 minutes) for symptomatic HFrEF+ID. Oral iron will not work reliably due to gut oedema and inflammatory iron absorption impairment. Expected benefit: improved NYHA class, 6-min walk distance, quality of life, and reduced HF hospitalisation. Re-check iron stores at 3 months; repeat infusion if ferritin <100 or TSAT <20%. 2. Consider AF catheter ablation (or rhythm control escalation) — AF+HFrEF with ongoing NYHA Class III despite GDMT is an indication for considering catheter ablation. CASTLE-AF data: AF ablation in HFrEF+AF significantly reduced mortality and HF hospitalisation and improved EF. With HR of 95 on bisoprolol, the AF may be contributing to his persistent Class III symptoms (residual tachycardia-mediated CMP component). Alternatively, ensure rate control is truly adequate (consider Holter to assess 24-hour mean HR — target <80 bpm, not just resting 95).
sections.title: Study text

sections.body:
Valvular disease causes HF, and HF causes secondary valvular disease. The relationship is bidirectional and critically important — because treating the valve can restore HF, while ignoring it keeps patients trapped in decompensation.

## Valvular causes of HF

### Aortic stenosis (AS) → HFpEF or HFrEF

Severe AS creates chronic pressure overload → concentric LVH → initially HFpEF (stiff LV, elevated filling pressures, preserved EF). As the disease progresses: myocyte death, fibrosis → decompensation → EF falls → HFrEF. The classic symptom triad (syncope, angina, dyspnoea) each predicts survival without intervention: syncope 3 years, angina 5 years, dyspnoea 2 years.

HF treatment in severe AS: medications alone are insufficient and can be harmful. ACEi/ARBs cause afterload reduction but in a patient with fixed outflow obstruction, they can cause haemodynamic collapse. Diuretics help symptoms but cannot address the fixed obstruction. Aortic valve replacement (SAVR or TAVR) is the only definitive treatment. After successful AVR, the LV can reverse-remodel — even patients with EF 25% from AS can recover to normal EF after valve replacement.

TAVR (transcatheter aortic valve replacement): now the dominant approach for severe AS in most patient groups. PARTNER 3, Evolut Low Risk, and multiple trials show TAVR equivalent or superior to SAVR in low-to-high surgical risk. Advantages: no sternotomy, faster recovery. Limitations: paravalvular leak, need for pacemaker (~10–20% for TAVR), valve durability (not yet established beyond 10–15 years).

### Mitral regurgitation (MR) → volume overload HFrEF

Primary MR (degenerative — prolapse, flail leaflet): the MR jet causes LV volume overload → eccentric hypertrophy → progressive LV dilation → EF falls. Surgery indications: severe primary MR with symptoms, OR asymptomatic with EF ≤60% or LVESD ≥40 mm (these thresholds indicate LV decompensation is beginning).

Secondary (functional) MR: the LV dilates from another cause (ischaemic CMP, DCM) → the annulus dilates + papillary muscles displaced → leaflets tethered → MR develops. The MR is a consequence of HF. Treatment: optimise GDMT first (reducing LV size reduces functional MR). MitraClip (transcatheter mitral valve repair): COAPT trial — in selected patients with severe secondary MR despite optimal GDMT: MitraClip significantly reduced HF hospitalisation and mortality. Selection criteria critical (EROA ≥0.4 cm², moderate-severe symptoms, EF 20–50%).

Key concept: Secondary MR in HFrEF: treat the HF first — the MR may improve as the LV shrinks with GDMT
In functional/secondary MR from dilated LV, the leaflets are structurally normal — they are simply being pulled apart by a dilated annulus and displaced papillary muscles. When GDMT reduces LV volume and reverses remodelling, the annulus narrows, papillary muscles return toward normal position, and MR severity decreases. Do not rush to recommend mitral intervention in newly diagnosed HFrEF+functional MR before optimising GDMT for ≥3 months. If MR persists at ≥3 months with optimal GDMT, then consider referral for MitraClip or surgical repair (if anatomy suitable).

### Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) and right HF

Severe TR in HF is increasingly recognised as an independent prognostic marker. Primary TR (flail leaflet, carcinoid, endocarditis) requires early repair/replacement before RV dilation occurs. Secondary TR (from pulmonary hypertension, RV dilation, AF) is managed by treating the underlying cause. Tricuspid repair/replacement has historically been avoided due to poor surgical outcomes in the context of advanced HF — transcatheter tricuspid repair (TRILUMINATE pivotal, CLASP TR) devices are emerging as lower-risk alternatives.

## Atrial defects and congenital disease in adult HF

ASD (atrial septal defect) causes left-to-right shunting → progressive RV volume overload → RV dilation → RV failure and pulmonary hypertension if unrepaired. Adults presenting with unexplained RV dilation or new AF should be evaluated for late-presenting ASD (particularly secundum ASD, which may be asymptomatic for decades). Transcatheter ASD closure is preferred over surgical repair in most adults with suitable anatomy.

Checkpoint: A 75-year-old woman with HFrEF (EF 28%, dilated CMP), NYHA Class III, on all four GDMT pillars, has severe secondary mitral regurgitation (EROA 0.45 cm²) confirmed on echo. She has been optimised on GDMT for 6 months without improvement in symptoms or EF. Her surgical risk is high (STS score 8%). What is the appropriate intervention and on what trial evidence?
MitraClip (transcatheter mitral valve repair) is the appropriate intervention based on the COAPT trial. The selection criteria are met: severe secondary MR (EROA ≥0.4 cm² = 0.45 cm²), HFrEF (EF 28%), NYHA Class III, ≥6 months of optimal GDMT without improvement (persistent severe MR despite optimal medical therapy — the crucial COAPT inclusion criterion). High surgical risk (STS 8%) makes open repair less appropriate. COAPT trial (2018): MitraClip vs optimal medical therapy alone in severe secondary MR — at 24 months, MitraClip reduced all-cause mortality by 38% and HF hospitalisation by 47%. The MITRA-FR trial (contemporaneous) showed no benefit, but COAPT's stricter selection criteria (including requiring disproportionately severe MR relative to LV volume) explain the discrepancy — patient selection is everything for MitraClip outcomes. This patient fits COAPT criteria. Refer to a heart valve team for percutaneous mitral repair.

sections.body:
Advanced HF is Stage D — refractory symptoms despite optimal medical and device therapy. The decisions here are among the hardest in medicine: who gets listed for transplant, who gets an LVAD, and who should be transitioned to palliative care.

## Defining advanced HF

The 2021 ESC guidelines define advanced HF by all four of:

1. Severe persistent symptoms (NYHA III–IV despite therapy)
2. Severe cardiac dysfunction: EF ≤30%, isolated RV failure, or inoperable valvular disease
3. Episodes of fluid retention or low cardiac output: ≥1 hospitalisation for HF in past 6 months, IV diuretic need, IV inotrope need, or profound limitation on exertion
4. All the above despite optimal GDMT, device therapy, and correction of precipitants

The "I NEED HELP" mnemonic (ESC 2019) identifies high-risk HF: Inotrope dependence, NYHA Class III/IV refractory, End-organ dysfunction, EF very low, Defibrillator shocks (appropriate), Hospitalisation >1/year, Edema (persistent fluid overload), Low systolic BP, Poor exercise tolerance. Meeting several criteria suggests Stage D HF requiring specialist advanced HF centre referral.

## Cardiac transplantation

### Indications for listing

- Stage D HF with predicted 1-year mortality >20% despite optimal therapy
- Recurrent life-threatening arrhythmias despite GDMT and ICD
- Refractory angina not amenable to revascularisation with severe LV dysfunction
- Prognosis better post-transplant than expected survival without (1-year post-transplant survival ~85%; 10-year ~50%)

### Contraindications — absolute

- Active malignancy (except localised skin cancer or certain cured cancers — tumour-free period typically 5 years)
- Active systemic infection
- Severe irreversible pulmonary hypertension (PVR >5 Wood units or transpulmonary gradient >15 mmHg fixed on vasodilator challenge) — the transplanted normal RV cannot handle a fixed high pulmonary resistance → donor RV failure → primary graft failure → death
- Active alcohol or substance misuse
- Severe irreversible end-organ dysfunction (hepatic cirrhosis — unless combined transplant; severe COPD)
- BMI >35 kg/m² (relative — significant perioperative risk)
- Age >70 years (relative — individual assessment based on biological age)

Key concept: Fixed pulmonary hypertension (PVR >5 Wood units irreversible) is an absolute contraindication to cardiac transplant
The donor heart comes from a normal person — the donor RV is a normal, thin-walled, low-pressure pump adapted to pulmonary vascular resistance of 1–3 Wood units. Transplanting it into a recipient with fixed PVR 6–8 Wood units means the donor RV immediately encounters resistance 3× higher than it was designed for → acute donor RV failure → primary graft dysfunction → the most common early cause of death post-transplant. Before listing, all transplant candidates have right heart catheterisation to measure PVR, and a vasodilator challenge (IV nitric oxide, prostacyclin, or nitroprusside) — if PVR reduces to <3 Wood units with vasodilators, transplant is feasible; if fixed even on maximal vasodilation → absolute contraindication → LVAD or palliative.

### Post-transplant management

- Immunosuppression: triple therapy — calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus or ciclosporin) + antiproliferative agent (mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine) + corticosteroids. Life-long.
- Rejection: acute cellular rejection (T-cell mediated) monitored by surveillance endomyocardial biopsy and managed with IV methylprednisolone. Antibody-mediated rejection (AMR) — more severe, managed with plasmapheresis, IVIG, rituximab.
- Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV): accelerated diffuse coronary atherosclerosis — the leading cause of death >1 year post-transplant. Unlike native CAD, CAV is diffuse, concentric, and progresses rapidly. Annual coronary angiography ± IVUS for surveillance. Statins are mandatory post-transplant (reduce CAV progression). CAV is the main reason 10-year survival is only 50%.
- Denervation: the transplanted heart has no autonomic innervation initially — it cannot mount a normal HR response to exercise (the heart relies on circulating catecholamines for rate increase). Resting HR is typically 90–110 bpm. Over years, some re-innervation occurs. This also means standard angina symptoms are absent in CAV — patients develop exercise intolerance or sudden death rather than angina.

## Palliative care in advanced HF

For patients who are not transplant/LVAD candidates and have Stage D HF, palliative care principles apply:

- Goals of care discussion: shift from "how do we extend life" to "how do we make the remaining time comfortable and meaningful." Document ADRT (advance decision to refuse treatment), DNACPR, and preferred place of death.
- ICD deactivation: patients near end of life should be offered ICD deactivation — repeated painful ICD shocks in the dying phase cause distress without prolonging meaningful life. This is an ethically appropriate and important discussion.
- Continuous subcutaneous infusion: SC furosemide (via syringe driver), opioids for dyspnoea, midazolam for anxiety/breathlessness — palliate symptoms in patients unable to take oral medications.
- Palliative inotropes: low-dose IV dobutamine or milrinone infusion — not to prolong life but to improve comfort and reduce dyspnoea in patients who cannot achieve adequate comfort on oral or SC medications. The patient may be discharged home with a portable inotrope pump.

Checkpoint: A 62-year-old man with ischaemic CMP (EF 18%) has been hospitalised 3 times in the past 6 months. He is on maximum GDMT and has a CRT-D. His last NYHA class was III–IV. Right heart catheter: CI 1.7 L/min/m², PCWP 28 mmHg, PVR 4.2 Wood units. Vasodilator challenge with inhaled NO: PVR drops to 2.8 Wood units. What are the two key conclusions from the catheter data, and what is the recommended next step?
Two conclusions: (1) Haemodynamic profile consistent with advanced HFrEF: CI 1.7 L/min/m² (<2.2 = low output) and PCWP 28 mmHg (>15 = severely elevated filling pressures) = "cold and wet" = Stage D with haemodynamic compromise — this patient meets advanced HF criteria. (2) PVR is elevated but reversible: baseline PVR 4.2 Wood units is above the transplant threshold of >5 Wood units, so it is borderline but not yet absolutely contraindicated. With NO challenge, PVR drops to 2.8 Wood units — this is vasodilator-responsive pulmonary hypertension, which means it is not fixed, and transplant is potentially feasible. Recommended next step: LVAD implantation as a bridge to transplant (BTT). The LVAD will: (a) provide immediate haemodynamic support (CI will increase to 4–6 L/min); (b) over time, reduce PCWP and reverse the reactive pulmonary hypertension further (many patients' PVR normalises completely after 3–6 months of LVAD support, opening the door to transplant). He can then be formally listed for transplant once haemodynamics improve on LVAD. Alternative if LVAD is declined: pursue transplant listing acknowledging borderline PVR with plan for re-RHC at 3 months.

sections.body:
The evidence base for GDMT was built in landmark trials that excluded many patients routinely seen in practice — pregnant women, the elderly, patients with severe renal disease. These populations require tailored thinking.

## HF in pregnancy — peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM)

PPCM is idiopathic DCM presenting in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months post-delivery in women without prior cardiac disease. Incidence ~1:1000–4000 deliveries in the West; much higher in West Africa and Haiti. Mechanism: bromocriptine-cleavage products of prolactin are toxic to cardiomyocytes; angiogenic imbalance; immune-mediated.

### Clinical features and diagnosis

Dyspnoea, oedema, orthopnoea in the peripartum period. Echo confirms dilated LV with reduced EF. BNP elevated. Apical thrombus in ~10% due to LV stasis — anticoagulate.

### Management

- During pregnancy: avoid ACEi/ARB (teratogenic — foetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, death). Use hydralazine + ISDN for afterload reduction. Beta-blockers (labetalol, metoprolol) safe in pregnancy. Diuretics carefully (reduce placental flow).
- Post-delivery: full GDMT including ACEi/ARNi + BB + MRA + SGLT2i (dapagliflozin — hold during breastfeeding). Add bromocriptine (2.5 mg BD for 2 weeks then 2.5 mg OD for 6 weeks) — BOARD trial, IPAC data: bromocriptine inhibits prolactin → reduces toxin → improves EF recovery.
- EF recovery: ~50–70% of PPCM patients recover EF to ≥50% within 6 months. Predictors of non-recovery: baseline EF <30%, severe LV dilation, late diagnosis, no bromocriptine.
- Subsequent pregnancy risk: ~20–30% risk of recurrence if prior PPCM (higher if EF did not fully recover). Counsel carefully before planning further pregnancies.

Warning: ACEi and ARBs are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. They cause fetal renal tubular dysplasia, oligohydramnios, limb contractures, and death. Women of childbearing age on ACEi/ARNi for HF must have reliable contraception and be switched to hydralazine + ISDN immediately upon discovering pregnancy. ARNi (sacubitril/valsartan) is similarly absolutely contraindicated. This applies to all trimesters — the renal developmental effects are most severe in the second and third trimesters.

## HF in the elderly

Most HF patients are >70 years. Several important considerations:

- HFpEF predominates: elderly patients, particularly women, are more likely to have HFpEF than HFrEF. Treatment targets comorbidities, SGLT2i, and careful diuresis.
- Frailty and polypharmacy: reduced tolerance to full GDMT doses. Start low, titrate slower, monitor more frequently. Frailty does not preclude GDMT — even frail elderly patients benefit from neurohormonal blockade.
- Falls and hypotension: ACEi/ARNi cause orthostatic hypotension → falls risk → fractures. Measure lying/standing BP. Consider lower target doses in frail patients.
- Renal function: eGFR tends to decline with age — many elderly patients have eGFR 30–45 and require modified GDMT dosing and closer electrolyte monitoring.
- ICD in the very elderly: benefit decreases with age due to competing causes of death. NCDR registry data: patients >75 years have proportionally more non-sudden deaths (HF progression, non-cardiac death) — the ICD prevents only one mode of death. Shared decision-making and realistic expectation-setting are essential.
- Digoxin: historically used for rate control in AF and HFrEF. DIG trial showed digoxin reduced HF hospitalisations but not mortality. In the elderly: narrow therapeutic index + reduced renal clearance = high toxicity risk. If used, target low serum levels (0.5–0.8 ng/mL) and recheck whenever renal function changes.

## HF with severe renal impairment (eGFR <30)

- ACEi/ARNi: can continue down to eGFR 20 with close monitoring. Below eGFR 20: hold and reassess (evidence base is limited).
- SGLT2i: approved down to eGFR 20. Glycaemic effect diminishes at low eGFR but cardiorenal benefits persist (DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY trials).
- MRA: withhold if eGFR <30 (hyperkalaemia risk is high).
- Furosemide: remains effective but doses must be substantially higher in CKD (furosemide must be filtered at the glomerulus to reach tubular secretion site — reduced eGFR → less drug at the site of action → higher doses needed). IV furosemide is more reliable.
- Haemodialysis: ultrafiltration via dialysis can rapidly decongestion HF+ESRD patients who are refractory to diuretics. Cardiorenal clinic co-management is optimal.

Checkpoint: A 34-year-old woman presents 6 weeks post-partum with progressive dyspnoea, bilateral ankle oedema, and orthopnoea. She is breastfeeding. Echo: EF 28%, dilated LV. She is distressed and asks if she will "get her heart back." What is the immediate medical management, and what specific additional drug should be started that targets the underlying mechanism of PPCM?
Diagnosis: peripartum cardiomyopathy (6 weeks post-delivery, no prior cardiac disease, dilated LV with EF 28%). Immediate management: (1) Diuretics (furosemide 40 mg OD or IV if significant congestion); (2) ACEi now safe post-delivery — start ramipril 1.25–2.5 mg OD (ACEi is safe post-partum but hold during breastfeeding — switch to hydralazine + ISDN if breastfeeding continues); (3) Beta-blocker — metoprolol 12.5 mg OD (labetalol if breastfeeding preference); (4) Anticoagulation — given EF 28% and recent peri-partum state with potential apical thrombus risk, LMWH or anticoagulation consideration while breastfeeding (DOACs transfer into breast milk — avoid until weaning); (5) Bromocriptine 2.5 mg OD — targets the PPCM mechanism. Prolactin cleaved by cathepsin D → 16-kDa fragment → cardiotoxic (promotes apoptosis, vasospasm, cardiomyocyte death). Bromocriptine suppresses prolactin → reduces toxin → promotes EF recovery. This requires stopping breastfeeding (bromocriptine inhibits lactation) — a difficult but medically important discussion. Prognosis: reassure her — ~50–70% of PPCM patients recover EF ≥50% with optimal treatment, especially if treated early.
sections.title: Study text

sections.body:
The expert clinician recognises HF not just from classic presentations but from subtle patterns, dangerous mimics, and the specific combinations of findings that demand immediate escalation. This chapter synthesises the whole guide into recognition patterns you can apply at the bedside.

## Pattern 1 — The masked HFpEF patient

Many HFpEF patients reach your clinic with a complaint of "breathlessness" after extensive pulmonary workup has been non-contributory. The cardiac origin is missed because:

- BNP is borderline (80–120 pg/mL) — often attributed to "mild elevation from obesity or renal impairment"
- Resting echo is reported as "normal" — EF preserved, "mild diastolic dysfunction grade I, no significant valvular disease"
- The patient is told the heart is fine and referred back to respiratory

What you do differently: Look at the combination — E/e' 12, LAVI 36 mL/m², PASP 38 mmHg, and a patient with HTN, AF, and BMI 34 is HFpEF until proven otherwise. The borderline BNP in an obese patient is relatively higher than it looks. Order exercise stress echo. If the PCWP rises to >25 mmHg with exercise — that is HFpEF. Start SGLT2i. Start treating the modifiable risk factors aggressively.

## Pattern 2 — New LBBB + dyspnoea = new HFrEF until proven otherwise

A patient presents with exertional dyspnoea, new LBBB on ECG. The question is always: which came first — the LBBB or the HF? In practice, the answer often does not matter initially:

- Order echo immediately — EF will either be reduced (confirming HFrEF) or be falsely low from LBBB dyssynchrony (may improve with resynchronisation)
- If EF ≤35% and LBBB ≥150 ms → start GDMT + plan CRT-D after 90 days if EF does not recover
- If EF 36–50% (mildly reduced or borderline) — HFmrEF: treat as HFrEF, reassess at 3 months
- The LBBB itself may be the cause (LBBB-induced dyssynchrony → dilated appearance with reduced apparent EF) — in some patients, CRT alone recovers EF from 30% to 55% (the dyssynchrony was the entire problem)

## Pattern 3 — The ECG+Echo paradox → think amyloid

Any time you see this combination: low voltage on ECG + thick walls on echo, cardiac amyloidosis must be your leading diagnosis. This is not a subtle finding — it is dramatic. Normal people with thick walls have high voltage. Voltage and wall thickness should move together. When they dissociate, something is infiltrating the myocardium and attenuating the electrical signal while thickening the wall.

Additional amyloid clues that, combined with the voltage-wall paradox, essentially confirm the diagnosis clinically: carpal tunnel syndrome, bilateral bilateral biceps tendon rupture (spontaneous), peripheral/autonomic neuropathy, macroglossia, periorbital purpura (AL amyloid). In an elderly man (wildtype ATTR) — carpal tunnel syndrome years before dyspnoea is the classic prodrome.

Key concept: The five HF presentations that demand immediate senior review or escalation beyond standard care
1. HF + systolic BP <90 despite IV fluids and diuresis stopped → cardiogenic shock, cold-wet profile → inotropes + urgent echo + MCS consideration
2. New ADHF with mechanical murmur (new harsh pansystolic or decrescendo diastolic) + haemodynamic instability → mechanical complication (acute MR from papillary muscle rupture, VSR, free wall rupture) → urgent echo, cardiac surgery involvement immediately
3. HFpEF + rapidly deteriorating with shock physiology + no congestion → constrictive pericarditis vs tamponade vs obstructive pathology (HOCM with dehydration) → urgent echo
4. HF + unexplained weight loss + biventricular failure + low-voltage ECG in an elderly patient → amyloidosis with advanced disease → DPD/PYP scan, haematology involvement for AL exclusion, tafamidis if ATTR
5. Young woman, post-partum, EF ≤25% + apical thrombus on echo → PPCM with high embolism risk → anticoagulate immediately, bromocriptine, full GDMT (avoiding ACEi/ARNi if still breastfeeding)

## Pattern 4 — The HF patient who deteriorates on "correct" treatment

You start a patient with apparent HFrEF on GDMT. They worsen. Consider:

- Is the EF classification correct? Was the echo done during tachycardia (artificially low EF)? Is this actually HCM with outflow obstruction that you started ACEi on (dangerous)? Is this amyloid (digoxin was given — dangerous)?
- Is there a new precipitant? New AF, new ischaemia, new infection — even if the initial workup was "negative"
- Is the beta-blocker worsening HFpEF? In a patient misclassified as HFrEF who actually has HFpEF, a beta-blocker that slows HR limits exercise tolerance
- Drug interactions? NSAIDs prescribed by another clinician (cause Na/water retention + AKI + interact with ACEi/MRA → triple whammy), sodium-heavy IV fluid supplementation, calcium supplements in amyloid

## Pattern 5 — RV failure masquerading as left HF

Isolated or predominant RV failure is a diagnostic trap. The patient has oedema, raised JVP, fatigue — but without the pulmonary oedema and orthopnoea typical of left HF. The CXR may be clear. BNP is elevated. The echo shows a dilated, hypokinetic RV, preserved or hyperdynamic LV (the LV is underfilled from reduced RV output, so it contracts vigorously on little volume).

Causes of predominant RV failure: severe pulmonary hypertension (PAH, chronic thromboembolic PH), RV infarction (inferior MI with RV involvement — see ACS guide), severe TR, arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy (ARVC), severe COPD (cor pulmonale), massive PE.

The danger: giving loop diuretics aggressively to a patient with predominant RV failure and no pulmonary congestion → reduces preload → the underfilled LV (dependent on RV output for filling) gets even less volume → forward output collapses → cardiogenic shock from over-diuresis. Treat the cause of RV failure; use diuretics cautiously.

## The 10 most dangerous drug errors in HF — a synthesis table

# | Error | Why it is dangerous
1 | Giving diltiazem or verapamil in HFrEF | Negative inotropy → further reduces EF → acute decompensation. MDPIT trial showed harm. Never use in HFrEF. Safe in HFpEF for rate control.
2 | Stopping beta-blocker abruptly in chronic stable HFrEF | Rebound SNS activation → tachycardia, arrhythmia, acute decompensation. If stopping is needed, wean over 2 weeks.
3 | Starting ACEi/ARNi simultaneously (not sequential wash) | ACEi + neprilysin inhibitor → bradykinin excess → angioedema. Mandatory 36-hour ACEi washout before starting sacubitril/valsartan.
4 | Combining ACEi + ARB (dual RAAS blockade) | ONTARGET: dual blockade → excess renal failure, hyperkalaemia, no added mortality benefit. Use one arm of RAAS only.
5 | Nitrates in obstructive HCM | Preload reduction → smaller LV → worsens LVOTO → haemodynamic collapse. Same mechanism as nitrates in RV infarction.
6 | Digoxin in cardiac amyloidosis | Binds amyloid fibrils → accumulates → toxicity at "therapeutic" levels. Absolutely contraindicated in all amyloid CMP.
7 | Dobutamine in obstructive HCM or Takotsubo with LVOTO | Increased contractility → worsens obstruction → haemodynamic collapse. Use phenylephrine (pure α) or fluids instead.
8 | ACEi/ARNi in pregnancy | Fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, death. Switch to hydralazine + ISDN + BB immediately when pregnancy confirmed.
9 | Aggressive diuresis in HFpEF | Stiff LV is preload-dependent. Over-diuresis reduces filling pressures below the critical threshold → CO falls → low output symptoms. Gentle diuresis for symptom relief only.
10 | Starting ICD within 40 days of acute MI | DINAMIT, IRIS: early ICD does not reduce mortality (the VF in early MI is ischaemia-driven, and revascularisation addresses this). The 40-day rule is mandatory.

## Red flags requiring same-day response

Alert: Same-day cardiology review or emergency admission:
• SpO₂ <92% with pulmonary oedema on CXR → NIV + IV diuresis + consider ITU
• New pansystolic murmur in post-MI patient with haemodynamic instability → suspect VSR or papillary rupture → urgent echo + surgery
• BP <90 mmHg + warm extremities + new fever in a patient with LVAD → driveline infection + possible sepsis → IV antibiotics + device team review
• Worsening oedema + declining renal function + stopped responding to furosemide → diuretic resistance → metolazone or consider ultrafiltration
• New AF in a patient with known HCM → rate control URGENTLY (loss of atrial kick + tachycardia in an obstructed outflow → haemodynamic collapse) → BB + consider cardioversion
• Any LVAD patient with new headache, focal neurology, or haematuria → pump thrombosis or stroke → LVAD team urgently

Checkpoint: A 78-year-old man with "HFpEF" (EF 55%) has worsening dyspnoea over 6 weeks despite doubling his diuretic dose. He weighs 6 kg more than 6 months ago. ECG: sinus rhythm, QRS 82 ms, low voltage in limb leads. Echo: EF 55%, bilateral wall thickening (IVS 18 mm, PW 17 mm), granular sparkling appearance, grade III diastolic dysfunction, bilateral atrial enlargement. NT-proBNP 4800 pg/mL. He takes digoxin 125 µg OD which was started 3 months ago for rate control in a brief AF episode. What is the single most urgent action and why?
STOP DIGOXIN IMMEDIATELY. The echo findings are diagnostic of cardiac amyloidosis: biventricular wall thickening (IVS 18 mm, PW 17 mm), granular sparkling appearance (amyloid deposit pattern on 2D echo), severe diastolic dysfunction grade III (restrictive filling pattern — amyloid stiffness), bilateral LA and RA enlargement (chronically elevated filling pressures), and the crucial ECG–echo paradox: low voltage on ECG despite massive wall thickening on echo. Amyloid protein absorbs the ECG signal while physically thickening the wall. The NT-proBNP of 4800 pg/mL reflects severely elevated wall stress. Digoxin binds avidly to amyloid fibrils, accumulating to toxic intracardiac concentrations despite serum levels that may appear "therapeutic." He requires digoxin level checked immediately; if elevated or symptoms of digoxin toxicity (nausea, visual changes, bradycardia, arrhythmia) are present → treat toxicity. Next steps: Tc99m-DPD scintigraphy (grade 2/3 uptake + negative serum/urine free light chains = ATTR confirmed). If ATTR confirmed → start tafamidis (stabilises TTR tetramer, reduces fibril deposition, mortality benefit in ATTR-ACT). Avoid ACEi if BP is low (autonomic neuropathy common in amyloid → hypotension). Use diuretics cautiously — the restrictive physiology is preload-dependent.

sections.body:
Heart failure questions are the highest-frequency category on cardiology residency examinations. They test mechanisms, drug choices, contraindications, and clinical reasoning simultaneously. This chapter builds your systematic approach, catalogues the top traps, and closes with a synthesis vignette that brings the entire guide together.

## The HF MCQ framework — five questions before answering

Before looking at the answer options, answer these five questions about the vignette:

1. Which HF subtype? (HFrEF ≤40% / HFmrEF 41–49% / HFpEF ≥50% / acute decompensated / cardiogenic shock) — this determines the entire drug framework
2. What is the specific cardiomyopathy? (ischaemic / dilated / hypertrophic / amyloid / peripartum / Takotsubo) — each has unique drugs that are helpful and unique drugs that are dangerous
3. Is there a contraindication hidden in the vignette? (low eGFR, K⁺ elevation, pregnancy, prior ICH, acute decompensation, concurrent medications) — the exam always puts one in
4. What is the ECG finding? (LBBB → CRT consideration; AF → rate control drug choice; low voltage → amyloid; sinus tachycardia → compensated HF) — ECG clues change the answer
5. What is the question actually asking? (mechanism / drug choice / contraindication / monitoring parameter / device eligibility / next step in diagnosis) — read this twice before selecting

## The HF trap library — 14 high-yield traps

# | Vignette signal | Trap answer | Why it is wrong / correct answer
1 | HFrEF patient admitted with ADHF, tachycardia, dyspnoea | "Start carvedilol 6.25 mg BD immediately" | Never start BB in acute decompensated HF. Decongest first (IV diuretics). Start BB only when stable and euvolaemic.
2 | ACEi prescribed for HFrEF → creatinine rises 25% at 2 weeks | "Stop the ACEi" | A ≤30% creatinine rise from ACEi is expected and acceptable — it reflects reduced intraglomerular pressure. Continue unless creatinine rises >30% or K⁺ >5.5.
3 | HFrEF patient, HR 72 bpm on max BB, asked about ivabradine | "Add ivabradine" | Ivabradine requires HR ≥70 bpm despite maximum tolerated BB in sinus rhythm. HR 72 is borderline — but the key word is "maximum tolerated." If BB dose is not yet maximum, increase BB first.
4 | Patient switches from ACEi to sacubitril/valsartan — started the same day | "This is appropriate — both reduce Ang II" | Requires 36-hour ACEi washout before ARNi. Combined bradykinin + neprilysin inhibition → angioedema risk. This is one of the highest-yield safety facts in HF.
5 | Thick-walled LV on echo + low voltage ECG in elderly man | "This is hypertensive cardiomyopathy, start ACEi" | ECG–echo voltage paradox = amyloid until proven otherwise. Confirm with DPD/PYP scan + light chains. Digoxin (which he might already be on) is dangerous — stop immediately if amyloid confirmed.
6 | HFrEF + EF 28% + LBBB QRS 162 ms + NYHA III + 3 months GDMT | "ICD alone (primary prevention criteria met)" | CRT-D is superior to ICD alone when CRT criteria are also met. LBBB ≥150 ms + EF ≤35% + NYHA II–III = Class I CRT indication. CRT-D provides both resynchronisation AND defibrillation. Never choose ICD-only when CRT criteria are met.
7 | Post-MI 3 weeks, EF 30%, no GDMT yet — asking about ICD | "ICD indicated — EF 30% meets primary prevention criteria" | Two barriers: (1) post-MI <40 days = no ICD yet (DINAMIT/IRIS); (2) not yet on GDMT — EF may recover with neurohormonal blockade. Reassess EF after ≥3 months of optimal GDMT, then decide on ICD.
8 | HCM patient with exertional dyspnoea + systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva | "Start amlodipine for the HTN-appearing hypertrophy" | DHP calcium channel blockers are contraindicated in obstructive HCM — they reduce afterload without rate control → reflex tachycardia → worsens LVOTO. Use beta-blockers (first line) or non-DHP CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem).
9 | HFpEF patient with worsening renal function on aggressive IV furosemide | "Continue aggressive diuresis to target dry weight" | HFpEF is preload-sensitive. Over-diuresis in HFpEF → SV falls as the stiff LV loses the high filling pressure it depends on. Creatinine rise + low BP + worsening fatigue in HFpEF on aggressive diuretics = over-diuresis. Reduce diuretics.
10 | Pregnant woman, 30 weeks gestation, new HFrEF EF 32% | "Start ramipril 2.5 mg OD for HFrEF" | ACEi/ARB/ARNi absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (all trimesters). Use hydralazine + ISDN + BB (metoprolol, labetalol). Diuretics if needed (carefully).
11 | ADHF patient, furosemide dose doubled, creatinine rises 30 µmol/L over 48h | "Stop furosemide — AKI developing" | Creatinine rise during effective decongestion is haemoconcentration, not true AKI, in most cases. Continue if patient is diuresing and decongesting. The question is whether the patient is improving clinically (less oedema, better oxygenation) despite the creatinine rise.
12 | Patient with HFrEF + AF + HR 88 on bisoprolol | "Add diltiazem for better rate control" | Diltiazem (non-DHP CCB) is contraindicated in HFrEF — negative inotrope → further EF reduction. Add digoxin for additional rate control in HFrEF+AF if BB alone insufficient.
13 | MRA prescribed for HFrEF → K⁺ rises to 5.2 mmol/L at 1 week | "Stop MRA permanently" | K⁺ 5.0–5.5 mmol/L = hold or reduce MRA dose, recheck in 1 week after dietary K⁺ adjustment or diuretic optimisation. Do not permanently discontinue unless K⁺ consistently >5.5. The mortality benefit of MRA is too large to abandon without effort to maintain it.
14 | Saxagliptin prescribed to a patient with HFrEF + T2DM | "Appropriate — DPP-4 inhibitors are safe in HF" | Saxagliptin specifically increases HF hospitalisation (SAVOR-TIMI). Use SGLT2i preferentially. If a DPP-4i is needed for glucose control, alogliptin or sitagliptin are lower risk (avoid saxagliptin specifically).

## The 6 most commonly tested mechanism questions in HF

1. Why does sacubitril/valsartan work better than enalapril in HFrEF? ARNi adds neprilysin inhibition → increases natriuretic peptides (BNP, ANP, bradykinin) → amplified natriuresis, vasodilation, anti-fibrotic effects — on top of RAAS blockade. PARADIGM-HF: 20% additional relative risk reduction beyond enalapril's already large benefit.
2. Why do SGLT2 inhibitors work in HF, even without diabetes? Multiple non-glycaemic mechanisms: natriuresis, NHE1 inhibition (↓ intracardiac Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ overload → ↓ arrhythmia, ↓ apoptosis), erythropoietic effect (↑ haematocrit → ↑ O₂ delivery), ketone body substrate provision (more efficient cardiac fuel), anti-fibrotic effects.
3. Why does eplerenone work better than spironolactone in men with HFrEF? Spironolactone is non-selective — blocks mineralocorticoid, androgen, and progesterone receptors → gynaecomastia, sexual dysfunction, menstrual irregularities. Eplerenone is highly selective for the mineralocorticoid receptor → same anti-fibrotic and anti-aldosterone benefit without sex hormone side effects. Use eplerenone preferentially in men.
4. Why is cardiac rehabilitation better than drug therapy for improving exercise capacity in stable HFrEF? Drugs reverse neurohormonal harm and prevent structural deterioration. Exercise training in cardiac rehab does something different: improves skeletal muscle mitochondrial function, aerobic enzyme capacity, and peripheral vascular reactivity — the muscles work more efficiently with less cardiac demand. The heart doesn't have to work as hard for the same physical output. HF-ACTION trial: supervised exercise training reduced mortality/hospitalisation and significantly improved QoL.
5. Why does AF cause more symptoms in HFpEF than in HFrEF? In HFpEF, the stiff LV depends heavily on the atrial kick (late active filling) to maintain adequate end-diastolic volume at acceptable filling pressures. AF removes this atrial kick. The stiff LV must now fill completely in early diastole (passive filling only) → either filling pressures rise dramatically, or SV falls → acute decompensation. In HFrEF with dilated LV, the atrial kick contributes relatively less (the dilated, compliant ventricle fills more easily).
6. Why does ICD not reliably prevent death in advanced cardiac amyloidosis? SCD in amyloid patients is often from electromechanical dissociation (PEA) — the conduction system is infiltrated by amyloid → the electrical activity dissociates from mechanical contraction. The ICD can terminate VF but cannot restore cardiac mechanical function in PEA. Additionally, the arrhythmia substrate in ATTR is different from ischaemic CMP — PEA is more common than VF as the mode of terminal cardiac event.

## High-yield synthesis vignette — the complete HF patient

Checkpoint: A 66-year-old man with T2DM, hypertension, and prior anterior MI (8 months ago) presents to your clinic for HF review. Current medications: aspirin 100 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, bisoprolol 2.5 mg OD, lisinopril 5 mg OD. Echo: EF 32%, dilated LV (LVESD 58 mm), anterior wall akinesis, moderate functional MR (EROA 0.28 cm²), LBBB on ECG (QRS 158 ms), NYHA Class III. BP 118/74, HR 68 bpm, K⁺ 4.3, eGFR 52. NTproBNP 2800 pg/mL. Identify five specific changes to his management, prioritised in order of mortality benefit.
Priority 1 — Switch lisinopril to sacubitril/valsartan (ARNi)
He is on lisinopril (ACEi) — PARADIGM-HF showed sacubitril/valsartan 20% further relative risk reduction compared with enalapril in patients like him (HFrEF, EF 32%, well-compensated on GDMT). Stop lisinopril → wait ≥36 hours → start sacubitril/valsartan 24/26 mg BD → titrate to 97/103 mg BD. This is the single highest-mortality-benefit switch available given the current regimen.
Priority 2 — Add MRA (eplerenone or spironolactone)
He is on only 3 of 4 GDMT pillars — no MRA. EMPHASIS-HF criteria met: EF ≤35%, NYHA II–III, on ACEi/ARNi + BB. K⁺ 4.3 and eGFR 52 are both safe to start. Add eplerenone 25 mg OD (preferred over spironolactone in men). Monitor K⁺ at 1 and 4 weeks. Expected benefit: ~37% additional relative risk reduction in CV death/HF hospitalisation.
Priority 3 — Add SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin)
Fourth pillar missing. eGFR 52 is well above the ≥20 mL/min threshold. T2DM coexists — SGLT2i addresses both HF and glycaemia. Start dapagliflozin 10 mg OD. Inform him about genital hygiene (mycotic infection risk). Expect reduction in HF hospitalisation and further eGFR protection (renoprotective effect).
Priority 4 — Assess for CRT-D (at next visit, after 3 months of optimised GDMT)
LBBB 158 ms + EF 32% + NYHA III despite GDMT = Class I indication for CRT-D. However, he has only been on bisoprolol 2.5 mg (far from maximum) and is missing two GDMT drugs. Optimise all four GDMT pillars first (3 months), then repeat echo. If EF remains ≤35% with LBBB ≥150 ms after full GDMT → proceed to CRT-D. If EF recovers above 35% → ICD eligibility only; if EF recovers above 50% → reassess, may not need device implant urgently.
Priority 5 — Titrate bisoprolol to maximum tolerated dose
Bisoprolol 2.5 mg OD is far below the target of 10 mg OD. BP is 118/74 (allows upward titration), HR 68 bpm (suggests tolerance of further upward titration). Double to 5 mg OD today with plan to titrate further at 2-week intervals. Regarding the functional MR (EROA 0.28 cm²): this is below the COAPT threshold of ≥0.4 cm² — do not refer for MitraClip yet. Optimise GDMT first (reduce LV size → reduce MR) and reassess MR severity at 6 months. The atorvastatin dose should be increased to 80 mg (high-intensity statin for post-MI patient — current 40 mg is subtherapeutic for very high-risk secondary prevention).

## The final HF exam checklist

Alert: Before every HF answer — verify:
✓ EF classified correctly (≤40% HFrEF / 41–49% HFmrEF / ≥50% HFpEF)
✓ All four GDMT pillars present in HFrEF (ACEi/ARNi + BB + MRA + SGLT2i)
✓ ARNi washout rule applied (≥36h ACEi-free before sacubitril/valsartan)
✓ BB not started in acute decompensation; not stopped abruptly in chronic HF
✓ ICD timing rules: ≥40 days post-MI, ≥3 months of optimal GDMT before reassessing EF
✓ CRT criteria: EF ≤35% + LBBB ≥150 ms + NYHA II–IV + sinus rhythm → CRT-D if also ICD eligible
✓ HFpEF: SGLT2i + treat comorbidities + gentle diuresis + no aggressive BB
✓ Amyloid: no digoxin (ever) + DPD/PYP scan for ATTR confirmation + tafamidis if confirmed
✓ HCM: no nitrates, no DHP-CCBs, no inotropes, no ACEi (obstructive) → BB first-line
✓ Pregnancy/PPCM: no ACEi/ARNi → hydralazine + ISDN + BB + bromocriptine post-delivery
✓ Iron deficiency check (ferritin <100, or 100–299 + TSAT <20%) → IV iron (not oral)
✓ AF in HFrEF: rate control with BB/digoxin (never diltiazem/verapamil in HFrEF)
✓ K⁺ monitoring: ACEi/ARNi + MRA + K⁺-sparing diuretic = triple whammy risk — check at 1 and 4 weeks
✓ Transplant contraindication: fixed PVR >5 Wood units = absolute contraindication (donor RV will fail)

sections.body:
HF classification serves two purposes: describing where a patient is now, and predicting where they are going. The EF-based subtypes determine which drugs work and which kill. The staging systems determine urgency of intervention.

## EF-based classification — the most clinically important distinction

Ejection fraction (EF) is the most powerful single number in HF management, not because it perfectly captures cardiac function, but because it defines which treatments are evidence-based:

Category | EF | Old term | GDMT mortality benefit? | Prevalence
HFrEF HF with reduced EF | ≤40% | Systolic HF | Yes — all four pillars (ACEi/ARNi, BB, MRA, SGLT2i) | ~45–50% of HF
HFmrEF HF with mildly reduced EF | 41–49% | "Grey zone" | Probable — trial data emerging (DELIVER subgroup, PARAGON-HF borderline data suggests benefit). ESC recommends considering all HFrEF therapies. | ~10–15%
HFpEF HF with preserved EF | ≥50% | Diastolic HF | Only SGLT2i (EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER) — no proven mortality benefit from ACEi, BB, or MRA | ~40–50%

Key concept: EF alone does not tell you how sick the patient is — it tells you which drugs to give
A patient with HFpEF (EF 60%) and NYHA Class III is sicker and more symptomatic than a patient with HFrEF (EF 35%) and NYHA Class I who is well-optimised on GDMT. EF classifies the pathophysiological mechanism and drug eligibility — not symptom severity or prognosis alone. The most dangerous error in HF management is giving a non-DHP calcium channel blocker (diltiazem, verapamil) to a patient with HFrEF. These drugs have negative inotropy that further reduces EF and worsen outcomes (MDPIT trial). They are contraindicated in HFrEF. They may be used in HFpEF where the goal is heart rate control in AF or symptom relief.

## NYHA functional classification — severity of symptoms

Class | Description | Clinical examples
Class I | No limitation of physical activity. Ordinary physical activity does not cause fatigue, palpitation, or dyspnoea. | HF detected incidentally (echo for another reason). Asymptomatic LV dysfunction.
Class II | Slight limitation. Comfortable at rest. Ordinary activity (climbing stairs, walking briskly) causes symptoms. | "I get breathless walking up two flights of stairs." Mild ankle oedema. Manages daily activities independently.
Class III | Marked limitation. Comfortable at rest. Less-than-ordinary activity causes symptoms. | "I can only walk slowly across the room before getting breathless." Dressing causes fatigue. Needs assistance with activities of daily living.
Class IV | Symptoms at rest. Unable to carry on any physical activity without discomfort. | Breathless lying flat. Resting oedema. Orthopnoea. May require hospitalisation. Some patients are breathless at rest constantly.

Clinical link: NYHA class is used to determine device eligibility and drug titration endpoints. ICD/CRT eligibility requires NYHA Class II–III (not Class IV — prognosis too poor for ICD benefit in ambulatory Class IV unless transplant/LVAD candidate). GDMT is initiated and titrated targeting maximum tolerated doses. NYHA improvement (from Class III to II or II to I) with GDMT indicates reverse remodelling — a very good sign.

## ACC/AHA stages — the disease continuum

The ACC/AHA staging system describes HF as a progressive disease, not just a symptomatic state. It classifies structural changes alongside symptoms:

Stage | Description | Clinical example | Action
Stage A (At risk) | Risk factors for HF but NO structural disease, NO symptoms | Hypertension, DM, CAD, family history of CMP — but normal echo | Treat risk factors aggressively. This is where prevention happens.
Stage B (Pre-HF) | Structural disease (echo abnormality) but NO symptoms of HF | Asymptomatic LV dysfunction (EF 38% post-MI), LVH on echo, moderate AS with normal EF | Start ACEi/BB for asymptomatic LV dysfunction. Monitor. Prevent progression.
Stage C (Symptomatic HF) | Structural disease WITH current or prior symptoms | The typical "heart failure patient" — dyspnoea, oedema, fatigue with structural disease on echo | Full GDMT. Device therapy assessment. Diuretics for symptom relief.
Stage D (Advanced HF) | Refractory symptoms despite optimal therapy, requiring special interventions | Recurrent hospitalisations, inotrope-dependent, considering LVAD or transplant | Advanced HF referral. LVAD evaluation. Transplant listing. Palliative care integration.

Exam tip: Exam trap: Stage B HF (asymptomatic LV dysfunction) should still receive ACEi and beta-blockers. The SOLVD Prevention trial showed that enalapril in asymptomatic LV dysfunction (EF ≤35%) reduced the development of symptomatic HF and mortality. Stage B is not a "do nothing" stage — it is the critical window when neurohormonal blockade can prevent progression to symptomatic HF. If an exam question describes a patient with EF 30% post-MI who has no symptoms — they still need ACEi + BB started.

Checkpoint: Two patients: Patient A — NYHA Class III, EF 28%, ischaemic CMP, on ACEi + BB + MRA + SGLT2i. Patient B — NYHA Class I, EF 58%, hypertensive heart disease, no HF medications. Which has more advanced ACC/AHA staging? Which has more severe NYHA class? What does this reveal about how these classification systems work?
Patient A is ACC/AHA Stage C (symptomatic HF with structural disease) and NYHA Class III (significant symptom limitation). Patient B is ACC/AHA Stage A/B (depending on whether echo shows structural changes from hypertension) and NYHA Class I. Patient A has more advanced ACC/AHA staging AND worse NYHA class. However, the key insight: Patient A is on optimal GDMT — their EF may improve to 40%+ with continued treatment (reverse remodelling), and their NYHA class may improve to I or II. Patient B, while currently asymptomatic, may progress to Stage C if hypertension is not treated — they need aggressive risk factor management now. The lesson: ACC/AHA staging is one-directional (you move forward through stages over years), while NYHA class is bidirectional (can improve or worsen depending on clinical status and treatment). GDMT is the intervention that moves patients in the right direction on both scales.

sections.body:
HF signs and symptoms are directly derived from two haemodynamic problems — elevated filling pressures (congestion) and reduced forward output (low CO). Every finding makes physiological sense once you know which side of the circulation it comes from.

## Two haemodynamic problems, two symptom groups

Backward failure — congestion (high filling pressures): When the LV fails, it backs up fluid into the pulmonary circulation → pulmonary oedema. When the RV fails (or the LV failure becomes biventricular), it backs up into the systemic venous circulation → peripheral oedema. Symptoms: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND, oedema, ascites, hepatomegaly. Signs: bibasal crackles, raised JVP, S3, peripheral oedema, pleural effusions.

Forward failure — low cardiac output: Insufficient cardiac output fails to meet tissue oxygen demand. Symptoms: fatigue, exercise intolerance, muscle weakness, cognitive impairment, cold extremities, anorexia, weight loss (cardiac cachexia in advanced HF). Signs: cool peripheries, prolonged capillary refill, low BP, narrow pulse pressure, tachycardia, oliguria, raised creatinine.

## Symptoms in detail

### Dyspnoea

The cardinal symptom of left heart failure. Elevated left-sided filling pressures → increased pulmonary capillary pressure → fluid leaks into the pulmonary interstitium → stimulates J-receptors and stretch receptors in the lung → dyspnoea. Grades from exertional to resting dyspnoea as HF progresses.

### Orthopnoea

Dyspnoea that worsens on lying flat. When supine, venous return from the legs is redistributed to the thorax → pulmonary venous pressure rises → previously borderline patients tip into pulmonary oedema. Ask: "How many pillows do you need to sleep?" Two or more pillows for cardiac reasons = orthopnoea. The number of pillows correlates with PCWP severity.

### Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (PND)

The patient wakes suddenly, 1–2 hours after falling asleep, gasping for air, needing to sit upright or go to a window for air. Mechanism: Redistribution of oedema fluid from dependent tissues (legs) back into the circulation during sleep → pulmonary congestion. PND is highly specific for left HF (specificity ~90%). Resolves after 15–30 minutes sitting upright.

### Bendopnoea

A less well-known but specific symptom: dyspnoea occurring within 30 seconds of bending forward (as when putting on shoes). Caused by increased abdominal compression of the IVC → increased venous return → elevated filling pressures → dyspnoea. Sensitivity ~27%, specificity ~92% for elevated PCWP. Ask this question in HF assessment.

Key concept: Orthopnoea and PND are highly specific for cardiac dyspnoea — distinguish HF from respiratory causes
A patient with COPD or asthma typically has dyspnoea with exertion and at rest without positional worsening (unless severe COPD with significant trapping). The position-dependent worsening of orthopnoea and PND is virtually diagnostic of elevated pulmonary venous pressure (left HF). In contrast, the dyspnoea of COPD and asthma may actually improve when the patient leans forward (tripod position — improves accessory muscle use). Positional dyspnoea that worsens supine = cardiac. Positional dyspnoea that improves supine = suspect asthma/COPD (breathing easier lying down due to reduced dead space, or tripod position no longer needed).

## Physical examination findings

### Raised JVP (Jugular venous pressure)

The JVP reflects right atrial pressure. In HF, elevated RA pressure from RV failure or biventricular failure elevates the JVP. Normal JVP: <4 cm above the sternal angle with the patient at 45°. Elevated JVP: the pulsations are visible above the clavicle at 45°.

Hepatojugular reflux (HJR): apply sustained pressure to the right upper quadrant for 10–15 seconds → if JVP rises and stays elevated >3 cm, the test is positive. Positive HJR indicates elevated right heart filling pressures that cannot accommodate additional venous return from the hepatic circulation. Sensitivity ~70%, specificity >90% for elevated PCWP (>15 mmHg).

Kussmaul's sign: JVP rises on inspiration rather than falling (normally it falls). Indicates the RV cannot accommodate the increased venous return of inspiration — seen in constrictive pericarditis, severe RV failure, tricuspid stenosis, and rarely severe cardiac tamponade.

### Third heart sound (S3)

A low-pitched sound heard in early diastole (after S2), 0.14–0.18 seconds after the second heart sound. Caused by sudden deceleration of blood flow as it fills a dilated, non-compliant LV during early rapid filling. The S3 is a highly specific sign of elevated LV filling pressure (PCWP >20 mmHg). S3 in adults ≥40 years = pathological (HF or cardiomyopathy). S3 in athletes <30 years may be physiological (high flow state).

### Fourth heart sound (S4)

A low-pitched sound in late diastole (before S1 — the "pre-systolic sound"). Caused by the atrial kick pushing blood into a stiff, non-compliant LV during atrial systole. S4 indicates diastolic dysfunction (stiff LV). Common in LVH (hypertension, HCM), ischaemia. Absent in AF (no organised atrial kick).

### The displaced apex beat

Normally felt at the 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line. In dilated cardiomyopathy or volume-overloaded LV, the apex is displaced laterally and inferiorly (LV has enlarged outward). Felt in the 6th ICS, anterior axillary line in severe dilation. A diffuse, heaving apex beat (feels like lifting your finger rather than a sharp tap) indicates LV enlargement and pressure overload. A tapping apex beat (sharp, not diffuse) suggests MS (non-dilated LV with normal or reduced stroke volume).

Diagram: Bedside HF examination — key signs, their physiological origin, and their clinical significance (drawing not carried over)

## The Forrester-Stevenson profiles — bedside haemodynamics

As discussed in the ACS guide, the clinical assessment at the bedside can classify patients into haemodynamic profiles that guide immediate management. In chronic HF, the same framework applies:

- "Warm and dry" (Profile A): compensated HF. No congestion signs, adequate perfusion. This is the target of GDMT — to keep patients here.
- "Warm and wet" (Profile B): congested but well perfused. Most common acute decompensation pattern. Responds well to diuretics + vasodilators.
- "Cold and dry" (Profile L): hypovolaemic or RV failure. Low perfusion without congestion. Fluid challenge first; reassess for RV failure.
- "Cold and wet" (Profile C): cardiogenic shock. Low perfusion AND congestion. Highest risk. Inotropes + vasopressors + possible MCS.

Checkpoint: On examination: JVP elevated 8 cm above sternal angle, bibasal crackles to mid-zones, bilateral pitting oedema to the knees, S3 on auscultation, HR 105 bpm, BP 110/85 (narrow pulse pressure). Apex beat displaced to 6th ICS, anterior axillary line. No cool extremities. Which Forrester-Stevenson profile, and what does the narrow pulse pressure tell you about cardiac output?
This is Profile B — "Warm and wet": elevated JVP, bibasal crackles, bilateral oedema, S3 (all signs of congestion) but warm extremities (no forward failure). The narrow pulse pressure (110 − 85 = 25 mmHg, normal >40) tells you: pulse pressure is a bedside surrogate for stroke volume. Low SV → small stroke ejected → low systolic peak → narrow pulse pressure. This patient has inadequate forward output (SV) despite the warm peripheries — the SNS is maintaining peripheral perfusion by vasoconstriction (hence warm) but the narrow pulse pressure reveals the low SV. The displaced apex (6th ICS, anterior axillary line) confirms significant LV dilation (eccentric hypertrophy from volume overload or dilated CMP). Management: IV furosemide for acute decongestion (see Chapter 8), review and optimise GDMT, echo urgently to confirm EF and guide treatment.
